DECK 02 · CORE FOUNDATIONS · SILBERSCHATZ CH. 1 & 2

Introduction to Operating Systems, Dual-Mode Hardware & OS Structures

Silberschatz 10th Ed. §1.1–§1.10 & §2.1–§2.10 (OS Structures §2.8 beyond Deck 02) · Core Topic Scope (Practice Q1.A, Q2.A)
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Contrast the User View (convenience / utilization / battery) with the System View (Resource Allocator & Control Program).
  • Trace Computer-System Organization: System Bus, Bootstrap Program, Interrupt Vector Table (IVT), Storage Hierarchy, and Direct Memory Access (DMA).
  • Compare Symmetric (SMP) vs. Asymmetric (AMP) Multiprocessing, Multi-core, NUMA, and Client-Server vs. Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Computing (§1.3, §1.10.3–§1.10.4).
  • Distinguish cleanly between Multiprogramming and Multitasking (Time-Sharing) (§1.4, Mock Midterm Q1.A).
  • Trace all 6 steps of Dual-Mode Operation (§1.4.2, Mode Bit 1 ↔ 0) during a system call trap and explain how hardware Timers (§1.4.3) stop infinite loops (Mock Midterm Q2.A).
  • Identify all 6 System Call categories (§2.3.3), 3 Parameter Passing methods, System Generation/Boot/Debugging (§2.9–§2.10), and OS Structure architectures (§2.8).
💡 Intuition-First Mental Model (Before the Formulas)
  • Naive Solutions → Visible Failure: Letting user apps talk straight to disks or run CPU instructions unchecked sounds fast—until one buggy while(1); freezes every user forever or one accidental pointer overwrite formats the OS kernel! Conversely, halting the CPU on every single byte of disk I/O via interrupts saturates CPU cycles on DMA bookkeeping.
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: Picture a bank vault with a armored teller window. User programs wait in the lobby (User Mode, Bit = 1) and slide a formal slip through the slot (Trap / Syscall); hardware flips the security deadbolt to Kernel Mode (Bit = 0), validates the ID via the IVT, accesses the vault, and resets Bit → 1 on exit. Where the analogy breaks: No human guard watches a runnable process inside an infinite loop—if the app never visits the teller window, control returns ONLY when a hardware countdown Timer (§1.4.3) physically hits zero and triggers a preemption interrupt!
  • Why Each Rule Exists: DMA = 1 interrupt per block amortizes trap overhead across thousands of bytes; Dual-Mode hardware ensures unprivileged user code can never touch page tables, interrupt lines, or the mode bit itself without trapping cleanly through kernel-verified entry points.

1. What is an Operating System? (Silberschatz §1.1)

A computer system divides cleanly into four components: Hardware (CPU, memory, I/O devices), the Operating System, Application Programs (compilers, browsers, databases), and Users (people, machines, other computers).

📜 Textbook Definition (Silberschatz §1.1)
"An operating system is a program that manages a computer's hardware. It also provides a basis for application programs and acts as an intermediary between the computer user and the computer hardware." — And structurally, the OS is defined operationally as the one program running at all times on the computer — the kernel (plus system programs and middleware).

User View

Single-user PC: Designed for ease of use and good performance; hardware utilization is secondary.
Mainframe/Shared Server: Maximizes hardware and CPU utilization so every user gets fair share.
Mobile/Handheld: Balances usability with strict battery life.
Embedded Systems: Runs with minimal or zero user interface.

System View

1. Resource Allocator: Decides between conflicting requests for CPU time, memory space, file storage, and I/O devices cleanly and fairly.
2. Control Program: Supervises execution of user programs to prevent errors and improper or unauthorized hardware use.

2. Computer-System Organization, Interrupts & Storage (§1.2)

A modern general-purpose computer consists of one or more CPUs and multiple device controllers connected through a common system bus that provides shared access to main memory. Each device controller manages a specific device type (disk, USB, display) and maintains a local buffer + status/control registers.

  • Bootstrap Program: The first code executed on power-up or reboot, stored in firmware (ROM / EEPROM). It initializes CPU registers, device controllers, and memory, then locates and loads the OS kernel into RAM.
  • Interrupt-Driven Execution: When a device controller finishes I/O, it asserts a signal on the interrupt-request line. The CPU immediately saves its current state (PC + registers), uses an index to look up the handler address in the Interrupt Vector Table (IVT) in low memory, jumps to the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR), and restores state upon completion.
  • Interrupt vs. Trap (Exception): Hardware triggers asynchronous interrupts (e.g., disk done, timer tick). Software triggers synchronous traps/exceptions either accidentally (division by zero, illegal memory access) or intentionally (executing a system call instruction like SVC / SYSCALL / INT 0x80).
  • Direct Memory Access (DMA): Interrupt-driven byte-by-byte I/O works well for slow devices (keyboards) but cripples CPU throughput on high-speed disks. With DMA, the CPU programs the DMA controller with source/destination addresses and byte count; the DMA controller transfers an entire block directly between device buffer and main memory via bus cycle stealing and raises only 1 interrupt per block.
STORAGE HIERARCHY (Silberschatz Fig. 1.4 — Top = Fastest, Costliest, Volatile; Bottom = Slowest, Cheapest, Nonvolatile) ┌───────────────────────────┐ Registers (< 1 ns, CPU internal, Volatile) ├───────────────────────────┤ L1 / L2 / L3 (1–15 ns, SRAM Cache, Volatile) ├───────────────────────────┤ Main Memory (50–100 ns, DRAM, Volatile — directly byte-addressable by CPU) ├───────────────────────────┤ NVM / NVMe SSD (10–100 µs, Flash/3D XPoint, Nonvolatile) ├───────────────────────────┤ Hard Disk (HDD) (4–12 ms, Magnetic platters, Nonvolatile) ├───────────────────────────┤ Optical / Tape (sec–min, Archival tertiary storage) └───────────────────────────┘ * Caching Rule: Information copied into faster storage temporarily; OS/HW must maintain Cache Coherency on multicore CPUs.

3. Computer-System Architecture & Multiprocessing (§1.3)

  • Asymmetric Multiprocessing (AMP): Boss-worker model; one master CPU schedules and assigns tasks to worker CPUs. Simpler kernel locking, poorer scaling.
  • Symmetric Multiprocessing (SMP): Each processor runs an identical copy of the kernel (peer relationship) and shares main memory + ready queues. Scales gracefully, requires careful synchronization.
  • Multi-core & NUMA: Putting multiple execution cores on a single silicon die speeds inter-core communication and lowers power compared to separate sockets. In large server topologies, NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) connects CPU groups via high-speed interconnect where local memory access is faster than remote socket access.
  • Clustered Systems: Multiple independent computers joined via SAN/LAN for High Availability (graceful degradation, asymmetric active-standby or symmetric active-active) and High-Performance Computing (parallel MPI workloads).

4. Multiprogramming vs. Multitasking (Mock Midterm Q1.A)

Wait until the CPU idles vs. preempt on a hardware clock tick—this distinction appears frequently on OS exams:

DimensionMultiprogramming (§1.4)Multitasking / Time-Sharing (§1.4)
Primary ObjectiveMaximize CPU utilization by keeping the CPU constantly busy with another job whenever the active job blocks.Minimize response time so interactive users can communicate with running programs concurrently.
CPU Switch TriggerPassive / Voluntary: switches only when the running process waits (e.g., performs an I/O request or terminates).Active / Preemptive: switches frequently via a hardware Timer Interrupt every few milliseconds (time quantum), even if the job is still computing.
User InteractionLow / Batch-oriented (no direct real-time user control during run).High / Interactive (requires virtual memory & process scheduling).

5. Dual-Mode Operation, Hardware Timers & Traps (§1.4.2–§1.4.3, Mock Midterm Q2.A)

Because the OS and user applications share the same hardware, a buggy or malicious user program could overwrite kernel code, loop forever, or issue rogue disk writes. Hardware solves this using a dedicated Mode Bit inside the CPU status register:

  • User Mode (Mode Bit = 1, Ring 3): Executes application code. Privileged instructions (HLT, CLI/enable-disable interrupts, changing Base/Limit or Page Table Base Register, switching Mode Bit, direct I/O port writes) are blocked by hardware and immediately trap to the OS.
  • Kernel Mode (Mode Bit = 0, Ring 0 — Supervisor / System / Privileged Mode): Full unrestricted hardware access inside the OS kernel.
  • Multimode Extension (§1.4.2): Modern CPUs add extra modes for Virtual Machine Monitors (VMM / hypervisors) so guest OSes believe they run in supervisor mode while still trapped by the host hypervisor.
  • Timer Protection (§1.4.3): Before dispatching a user process, the OS loads a programmable Hardware Timer (fixed or variable countdown). Every clock tick decrements the counter; hitting 0 raises a timer interrupt that flips Mode Bit → 0 and returns control to the OS scheduler—making it impossible for a user program's while(1); to freeze the CPU permanently.
⚠️ Mock Midterm Q2.A — Exact 6 Diagram Labels (Silberschatz Fig. 1.13)

Mock Midterm Q2.A reproduces Silberschatz 10th Ed. Fig. 1.13 (Transition from user to kernel mode) and blanks out the exact 6 step labels around user process executing (Mode Bit = 1) ↔ kernel:

  1. Blank 1 (User exit): calls system call — User process requests an OS service via trap opcode.
  2. Blank 2 (Transition down to Kernel): trap / mode bit = 0 — CPU hardware atomically clears Mode Bit 1 → 0 and indexes the IVT.
  3. Blank 3 (Bottom-right Kernel box): kernel mode (mode bit = 0) — Kernel now holds full Ring 0 privileges.
  4. Blank 4 (Inside Kernel): execute system call — Kernel validates arguments and runs the requested service routine.
  5. Blank 5 (Transition up to User): return / mode bit = 1 — Privileged return instruction resets Mode Bit 0 → 1.
  6. Blank 6 (User resume): return from system call — User process resumes at the instruction right after the syscall.

6. Computing Environments: Client-Server vs. Peer-to-Peer (§1.10.3–§1.10.4, Midterm Quick Guide HIGH)

DimensionClient–Server Computing (§1.10.3)Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Computing (§1.10.4)
Node RolesStrict separation: specialized Servers respond to requests from passive/smart Clients.Symmetric Peers: no fixed client/server distinction; any node acts as client, server, or both.
Variants / Service DiscoveryCompute-server (clients request computation/DB queries) & File-server (clients store/retrieve files).Joins P2P network via either (1) Central Lookup Service (e.g., Napster) or (2) Broadcast Discovery Protocol (e.g., Gnutella).
Bottleneck / ResilienceCentral server can become a single point of failure or traffic bottleneck.Decentralized scalability; resilient to single-node failure (e.g., Gnutella, BitTorrent, Skype VoIP).

7. System Calls, SYSGEN, System Boot & OS Structures (Silberschatz Ch. 2)

System Calls (§2.3–§2.3.3) provide the programmatic interface to OS kernel services (typically invoked via standard APIs like POSIX libc, Win32, or Java JVM rather than raw assembly traps for portability). Parameter passing uses: (1) CPU Registers (fastest, limited count), (2) Memory Block / Table (start address in a register, unlimited size), or (3) Stack (pushed by user, popped by OS).

System Call Category (§2.3.3)Representative POSIX / Windows Calls
1. Process Controlfork(), exec(), exit(), wait(), CreateProcess(), ExitProcess()
2. File Managementopen(), read(), write(), close(), unlink(), CreateFile()
3. Device Managementioctl(), read(), write(), request/release device, attach/detach
4. Information Maintenancegetpid(), alarm(), time(), sleep(), SetTimer()
5. Communications (IPC)pipe(), shm_open(), mmap(), socket(), send(), recv()
6. Protectionchmod(), umask(), chown(), SetFileSecurity()
  • OS Generation — SYSGEN (§2.9.1 / Slide 02 P117): Configures an OS distribution for specific hardware before building/installing (querying CPU model/options, installed RAM size, attached devices/addresses, and desired OS options).
  • System Boot (§2.9.2 / Slide 02 P118): Starts a computer by loading the kernel using a tiny firmware bootstrap program (stored in ROM/EEPROM/UEFI, often two-step via boot loader) that initializes hardware and transfers control to the kernel in Ring 0.
  • OS Debugging & Tuning (§2.10 / Slide 02 P97): User-process crash writes a core dump (memory image); OS crash writes a crash dump (kernel memory image), alongside performance counters and kernel tracing (DTrace / BCC).

Operating System Structures (§2.8 — [Textbook Beyond Slide 02]):

  • Monolithic Kernel (Traditional UNIX, Linux): Almost all OS functionality (scheduling, VFS, drivers, networking) runs inside a single kernel address space. Pro: Ultra-fast direct function calls with minimal context-switch overhead. Con: Hard to maintain; a single driver bug can panic the entire system.
  • Layered Approach: Hardware at Layer 0 up to User Interface at Layer N; each layer uses services only from lower layers. Pro: Clean debugging/modularity. Con: Defining strict acyclic layers is hard, and crossing multiple layers degrades I/O speed.
  • Microkernel (Mach, QNX): Removes all non-essential services out of Ring 0 into User-Space servers, leaving only minimal IPC, basic scheduling, and memory management in the kernel. Pro: Extensible, portable, fault-isolated, high security. Con: Frequent IPC user↔kernel context switches reduce throughput.
  • Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs — Modern Linux, Solaris, macOS): Object-oriented core kernel dynamically loads drivers/filesystems at runtime via module interfaces—combines monolithic call speed with microkernel modularity without IPC overhead.
  • Hybrid Systems (macOS Darwin, Windows, Android): Combines Mach microkernel + BSD monolithic layer + I/O Kit modules (macOS), or modified Linux kernel + ART VM + binder IPC framework (Android).

deck_03.html:
DECK 03 · EXECUTION UNITS · SILBERSCHATZ CH. 3 & 4

Processes, PCB, Context Switching, fork() Trees, IPC & Multithreading

Silberschatz 10th Ed. §3.1–§3.6 & §4.1–§4.3 (Zombies/Orphans/2n/Amdahl beyond Deck 03) · Core Topic Scope (Practice Q1.B, Q2.B, Q2.C)
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Distinguish a passive Program (executable on disk) from an active Process and sketch its 4 runtime memory sections.
  • Enumerate all fields of the Process Control Block (PCB) (§3.1.3) and trace why Context Switching is pure overhead (§3.2.3). (Note: the 5-state diagram & schedulers appear in Slide 04 / §3.1.2.)
  • Trace fork(), exec(), wait(), Cascading Termination (§3.3.2), plus extended textbook rules (2n trees, Zombie, Orphan).
  • Compare Shared Memory (§3.5) vs. Message Passing (§3.6) IPC (Mock Midterm Q1.B) and bounded vs. unbounded buffers (§3.5.1).
  • Diagram Single-Threaded vs. Multithreaded Processes (§4.1), distinguish Concurrency vs. Parallelism and Data vs. Task Parallelism (Mock Q2.B/C), Amdahl's Law, and the 3 Multithreading models (§4.3).
💡 Intuition-First Mental Model (Before the Formulas)
  • Naive Solutions → Visible Failure: Spawning a heavy cloned process for every single web request duplicates entire page tables, heap state, and kernel PCBs—and passing megabytes via kernel syscalls forces double-copy trips into and back out of Ring 0 on every read/write!
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: Shared Memory (§3.5) is a shared office whiteboard in the hallway: an admin unlocks the door once, and teams scribble directly at full speed (until two scribble on the same line without a mutex!). Message Passing (§3.6) is an inter-office courier: every envelope passes through the mailroom (kernel), slower per letter yet works cleanly across separate buildings (distributed machines!). Meanwhile, Threads (§4.1) are cooks sharing one kitchen (Code, Data, Files) with their own apron and spoon (PC, Registers, Stack). Where the analogy breaks: Shared memory relies on virtual page-table pointers mapping two processes' virtual pages to the exact same RAM frames, not contiguous hardware memory! And throwing 64 CPU cores at code with a 20% serial bottleneck hits Amdahl's 1/S = 5× brick wall like 64 cashiers sharing 1 receipt printer.
  • Why Each Formula Exists: Unconditional fork() doubles active callers each call giving 2n; Amdahl's Law 1 / [S + (1 − S)/N] models total elapsed runtime directly as fixed serial time S plus shrunk parallel time (1 − S)/N.

1. Process Concept & Memory Layout (§3.1)

A program is a passive entity stored on disk (executable binary). Once loaded into RAM, it becomes an active process owning a Program Counter (PC), registers, open files, and a virtual address space divided into 4–5 distinct sections:

HIGH ADDRESS ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ STACK (grows DOWN ↓) │ ← Local vars, function params, return addresses │ ↓ [Free Virtual Address Space] ↑ │ (Overflow if Stack meets Heap) │ HEAP (grows UP ↑) │ ← Dynamic memory: malloc(), calloc(), new ├────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ UNINITIALIZED DATA (BSS) │ ← Uninitialized global/static vars (zero-filled) │ INITIALIZED DATA │ ← Initialized global and static variables ├────────────────────────────────────────┤ LOW ADDRESS │ TEXT (Code Segment) │ ← Compiled machine instructions (read-only) └────────────────────────────────────────┘

2. The 5-State Process Lifecycle (§3.1.2)

Process StateMeaning & Hardware StatusOutgoing Transitions
NewProcess is being created (allocated PID & PCB).Admitted → Ready (by Long-Term Scheduler)
ReadyLoaded in RAM, awaiting CPU allocation on Ready Queue.Scheduler Dispatch → Running (Short-Term Scheduler)
RunningInstructions currently executing on a CPU core.Exit → Terminated | Interrupt → Ready | I/O or Event Wait → Waiting
Waiting (Blocked)Cannot execute until an external event completes (disk read, mutex, timer sleep).I/O or Event Completion → Ready
TerminatedExecution finished (exit()); OS reclaims resources once parent calls wait().Reaped from process table.

Exam Trap: Only one process per CPU core can be in the Running state at any instant, whereas many processes may sit simultaneously in Ready and Waiting queues. Also, a process cannot jump directly from Waiting → Running; it must pass through Ready first!

3. Process Control Block (PCB) & Context Switch (§3.1.3 & §3.2)

Inside the OS kernel, every process is represented by its PCB (called task_struct in Linux), containing: (1) Process State, (2) Program Counter, (3) CPU Registers, (4) CPU Scheduling Info (priority, queue pointers), (5) Memory-Management Info (base/limit registers, page tables), (6) Accounting Info (CPU time used, time limits, PID/PPID), and (7) I/O Status Info (allocated devices, open file table).

During a Context Switch from P0 to P1: (1) interrupt/trap occurs, (2) OS saves P0's registers & PC into PCB0, (3) OS restores P1's state from PCB1, (4) CPU resumes P1. Pure Overhead: The CPU executes zero useful application work during a context switch (speed ranges from microseconds to sub-millisecond depending on register set size & TLB flushes).

4. Process Creation (fork/exec), Termination & Extended Process States (§3.3)

pid_t pid = fork();
if (pid < 0) {
    fprintf(stderr, "Fork Failed");
} else if (pid == 0) {   /* Child Process */
    execlp("/bin/ls", "ls", NULL);  // Replaces child's memory image! Never returns on success
} else {                 /* Parent Process */
    wait(NULL);          // Parent blocks until child finishes & reaps exit status
    printf("Child Complete\n");
}
  • Parent-Initiated Termination & Cascading Termination (§3.3.2 / Slide 03 P47): A parent can abort a child (abort() / TerminateProcess()) if the child exceeded allocated resources, its assigned task is no longer needed, or the parent itself is exiting and the OS does not permit orphaned children. When terminating a parent forces the OS to automatically terminate all its children (and grandchildren), this is called Cascading Termination.
  • Sequential fork() Formula [Textbook Beyond Slide 03]: If a program executes n unconditional fork() calls in sequence (e.g., fork(); fork(); fork();), it creates 2n total processes (1 original + 2n − 1 newly created descendants). Watch for conditional branches (if (fork() == 0)) which produce fewer!
  • Zombie Process [Textbook §3.3.2 Beyond Slide 03]: A child has called exit() and freed its RAM, yet its entry (PID + exit code) lingers in the kernel process table because the parent is still alive and has not called wait(). Reaping prevents PID exhaustion.
  • Orphan Process [Textbook §3.3.2 Beyond Slide 03]: The parent terminates before the child without calling wait(). UNIX/Linux immediately reparents the orphan child to PID 1 (init / systemd), which periodically calls wait() to reap it when it finishes.

5. IPC: Shared Memory vs. Message Passing (Mock Midterm Q1.B, §3.5–§3.6)

Independent processes never share state; Cooperating processes exchange data for information sharing, computation speedup, modularity, and convenience via two core IPC models (plus the Producer–Consumer paradigm: Unbounded-Buffer puts no practical limit on buffer size so consumer only waits when empty; Bounded-Buffer fixes capacity so producer also waits when full):

CriterionShared Memory (§3.5)Message Passing (§3.6)
Kernel InvolvementKernel required only at setup (shm_open + mmap) to attach a shared region; afterwards reads/writes happen directly at full RAM speed.Kernel invoked on every transfer via send() / recv() system calls (higher syscall/copy overhead).
SynchronizationDeveloper's responsibility (mutexes/semaphores required to prevent race conditions).Handled implicitly by OS kernel queues/mailboxes.
Best Use CaseLarge data volumes between local processes on the same machine.Small control messages and distributed systems across networks.

Message Passing Design Choices (§3.6): (1) Naming (§3.6.1): Direct (send(P, msg) / symmetric vs asymmetric) vs. Indirect via Mailboxes/Ports (send(A, msg)); (2) Synchronization (§3.6.2): Blocking send + Blocking recv = Rendezvous (zero-capacity buffer), vs. Nonblocking async variants; (3) Buffering (§3.6.3): Zero capacity (queue=0, sender blocks), Bounded capacity (N, blocks if full), Unbounded capacity (sender never blocks).

6. Threads, Diagrams, Parallelism & Amdahl's Law (Ch. 4, Mock Midterm Q2.B/C)

A Thread is the basic unit of CPU utilization. Single- vs. Multithreaded Process Figure (§4.1 / Quick Guide HIGH): All threads inside one process share Code, Data, and Open Files (plus Heap), whereas each thread owns its own private Registers, Program Counter (PC), and Stack (making thread creation & switching ~10–100× cheaper than full processes).

Concurrency vs. Parallelism

Concurrency: Supports multiple tasks making interleaved progress (possible even on a 1-core CPU via time-slicing).
Parallelism: Executes multiple tasks simultaneously at the exact same physical instant across multiple hardware cores.

Data vs. Task Parallelism (Mock Q2.B/C)

Data Parallelism: Distributes subsets of the same data across cores applying the same operation (Mock Q2.C: adding 5 to each element of a 1,000-number array split across 4 cores = 250 each).
Task Parallelism: Distributes threads/tasks across cores performing different operations on the same or different data.

Amdahl's Law (§4.2.1 — [Textbook Beyond Slide 03]): Speedup ≤ 1 / [ S + (1 − S) / N ] S = serial fraction of program (0 ≤ S ≤ 1); N = number of processing cores. Even as N → ∞, maximum Speedup is capped at 1 / S!
  • Many-to-One: Many user threads → 1 kernel thread. Fast user switching, but 1 blocking syscall blocks entire process and zero multi-core parallelism.
  • One-to-One (Linux, Windows): Each user thread → 1 kernel thread. True multi-core parallelism + non-blocking on syscall, slight creation overhead.
  • Many-to-Many / Two-Level: Multiplexes M user threads onto N ≤ M kernel threads, allowing flexible concurrency without excessive kernel thread overhead.

DECK 04 · SCHEDULING DISPATCH · SILBERSCHATZ CH. 3 & 5

Process Schedulers, CPU Criteria, Dispatcher Latency & FCFS

Silberschatz 10th Ed. §3.2 & §5.1–§5.3.1, §5.8.2 · Deck 04 & Practice Q6.A
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Compare Slide 04's 2-State, 3-State, and 5-State Process Models, Scheduling Queues (Job, Ready, Device), and Long / Medium / Short-Term Schedulers (Midterm Quick Guide HIGH).
  • Understand the alternating CPU–I/O Burst Cycle and the empirical hyperexponential burst histogram (§5.1.1).
  • Classify all 4 Scheduling Circumstances as strictly non-preemptive vs. preemptive (§5.1.3).
  • Measure Dispatch Latency inside the short-term dispatcher (§5.1.4).
  • Master all 5 Scheduling Criteria + formulas (Utilization, Throughput = N / TotalSpan, TAT, WT, RT) and Little's Formula (§5.2, §5.8.2).
  • Draw the Ready Queue (0.5 marks on Mock Q6.A) + FCFS Gantt charts (including CPU idle gaps!), apply AT=0 / PID tie rules, and diagnose the Convoy Effect (§5.3.1).
💡 Intuition-First Mental Model (Before the Formulas)
  • Naive Solutions → Visible Failure: Letting every runnable program flood RAM without an admission filter (no Long-Term Scheduler) causes thrashing, while pure FCFS lets one 24 ms batch truck block two 3 ms motorcycles in a single tunnel—blowing average wait time up by nearly 6×!
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: Picture a DMV + single coffee counter. The Long-Term Scheduler (minutes) decides how many customers enter the lobby (degree of multiprogramming); the Medium-Term Scheduler temporarily escorts idle visitors outside (swapping) if the lobby overfills; the Short-Term Scheduler (milliseconds) calls the next seated customer to the teller counter! Under FCFS, anyone holding a 50-item grocery cart forces express shoppers to wait behind them. Where the analogy breaks: Real processes leave the counter every few milliseconds to wait on disk I/O (CPU–I/O burst cycle) and must also follow explicit exam tie-breakers (earliest AT, then smaller PID unless inverted!).
  • Why Each Formula Exists: TAT = CT − AT measures total wall-clock endurance; WT = TAT − BT isolates pure wasted ready-queue delay; Throughput = N / (CTmax − ATmin) measures completions over the active window (critical when all arrivals start at AT > 0!).

1. Slide 04 Foundations: Process Models, Queues & 3 Schedulers (§3.2 / Slide 04 P4–P15)

  • Evolution of Process State Models: 2-State (Running / Not Running) → 3-State (Running / Ready / Waiting) → 5-State (New → Ready ↔ Running ↔ Waiting → Terminated).
  • Scheduling Queues (§3.2.1): Job Queue (all processes in the system), Ready Queue (processes in RAM awaiting CPU), and Device Queues (per-I/O-device queues waiting on disk/printer).
  • Long-Term (Job) Scheduler: Invoked infrequently (seconds/minutes, may be slow); admits jobs from disk into Ready Queue and controls the degree of multiprogramming (balancing I/O-bound + CPU-bound mix).
  • Short-Term (CPU) Scheduler: Invoked frequently (milliseconds, MUST be fast); selects which Ready process executes next and assigns the CPU (sometimes the only scheduler in UNIX/Windows).
  • Medium-Term Scheduler (Swapping): Added when degree of multiprogramming must decrease; swaps processes out to disk and later back into RAM to free memory contention.

2. CPU–I/O Burst Cycle & Dispatcher (§5.1.1, §5.1.4)

Process execution alternates continuously between CPU execution bursts and I/O wait bursts, always starting and ending with a CPU burst (ending in an exit() system call). An I/O-bound program produces many very short CPU bursts; a CPU-bound program produces fewer, very long CPU bursts.

Whenever the CPU becomes idle, the Short-Term Scheduler (CPU Scheduler) picks a Ready process (FIFO queue, priority queue, tree, or unordered list), and the Dispatcher (§5.1.4) gives it physical control of the core by: (1) switching context, (2) switching to User Mode, and (3) jumping to the saved PC location. The time taken to stop one process and start another is Dispatch Latency (kept in microseconds).

3. Preemptive vs. Non-Preemptive Scheduling: The 4 Circumstances (§5.1.3)

#Transition CircumstanceType
1Running → Waiting (e.g., I/O request or wait() call)Non-preemptive (process cannot continue anyway)
2Running → Ready (e.g., timer interrupt expires)Preemptive choice
3Waiting → Ready (e.g., I/O finishes & preempts lower-prio process)Preemptive choice
4Running → Terminated (process calls exit())Non-preemptive (process finished)

Non-preemptive (Cooperative): Scheduling only under 1 & 4; once a process gets the CPU, it keeps it until blocking or terminating. Preemptive: Scheduling also under 2 & 3; essential for responsive OSes, but introduces race conditions on shared kernel data and requires synchronization (mutexes/interrupt disabling) inside kernel mode.

4. The 5 Core Scheduling Criteria & Little's Law (§5.2, §5.8.2)

TAT = Completion Time (CT) − Arrival Time (AT)  |  Throughput = N / (CTmax − ATmin)
WT = Turnaround Time (TAT) − Burst Time (BT)  |  RT = First CPU Start − AT For non-preemptive schedules (1 continuous block per job), Waiting Time equals Response Time (WT = RT). Once preemption splits execution, WT ≥ RT!
  • CPU Utilization (MAXIMIZE): Percentage of time the CPU stays busy doing useful work (typically 40% lightly loaded to 90% heavily loaded).
  • Throughput (MAXIMIZE): Number of processes completed per unit time: N / (CTmax − ATmin) (Slide 04 P26–P98; note truncation to 2 decimals like 3 / 31 = 0.09 in slides!).
  • Turnaround Time (TAT — MINIMIZE): Total interval from submission (Arrival) to completion, summing ready-queue wait, CPU bursts, and I/O waits.
  • Waiting Time (WT — MINIMIZE): Total time spent waiting purely inside the Ready Queue (CPU scheduling only controls WT directly!).
  • Response Time (RT — MINIMIZE): Time from submission until the first response starts being produced—critical for interactive UIs.
  • Little's Formula (§5.8.2 Queueing Models): In any steady-state queue, average queue length n = average arrival rate λ × average wait time W (n = λ · W). E.g., if 7 processes arrive per second and there are always 14 processes waiting in queue, average wait W = 14 / 7 = 2 seconds.

5. First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) & Slide 04 Worked Examples (§5.3.1)

⚠️ Exam Checklist (Mock Q6.A & Midterm Quick Guide)
  1. Draw the Ready Queue! Mock Midterm Q6 explicitly awards 0.5 marks per algorithm solely for drawing the Ready Queue order alongside Gantt (1.5), Table (1), Avg WT (0.5), and Avg TAT (0.5).
  2. Exam Conventions: If AT is omitted, assume AT = 0; equal arrival + equal priority ties break by smallest PID first unless the prompt overrides; read every priority direction twice!

FCFS allocates the CPU strictly in the order processes request it using a simple FIFO queue. It is easy to code and starvation-free, non-preemptive, and produces terrible average waiting time when burst sizes vary.

6. The Convoy Effect (§5.3.1)

📜 Textbook Definition: Convoy Effect
"All the other processes wait for the one big CPU-bound process to get off the CPU. This effect results in lower CPU and device utilization than might be possible if the shorter processes were allowed to run first."

Think of multiple short interactive/I/O-bound processes idling while one CPU hog holds the single processor, leaving disk controllers idle while the I/O processes queue up behind it; then when the CPU hog finally enters I/O, all tiny processes sprint through the CPU in microseconds and stampede onto the I/O queue together, starving the CPU!

DECK 05 · OPTIMAL NON-PREEMPTIVE SCHEDULING · SILBERSCHATZ §5.3.2

Shortest-Job-First (SJF) & Exponential Averaging Burst Prediction

Silberschatz 10th Ed. §5.3.2 (Exponential Averaging beyond Deck 05) · Deck 05 Practice Scope
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Explain why non-preemptive SJF (Shortest-Next-CPU-Burst) is provably optimal for minimum average waiting time.
  • Apply the tie-breaking rule (FCFS arrival order, then smaller PID in Slide 05) when ready processes share identical CPU burst lengths.
  • Solve Deck 05 SJF practice examples (Ex 01–04) including CPU idle intervals and Throughput.
  • Compute next CPU burst predictions via Exponential Averaging and interpret α = 0, α = 1, and α = 0.5 [Textbook §5.3.2 Beyond Slide 05].
💡 Intuition-First Mental Model (Before the Formulas)
  • Naive Solutions → Visible Failure: Letting one 24 ms CPU hog finish before two 3 ms jobs forces BOTH short jobs to suffer 24+ ms of wait! Putting any shorter burst before a longer ready burst eliminates a strictly larger delay than it creates—and guessing next burst from only the last burst (α = 1) overreacts to one random spike, whereas freezing at τ0 (α = 0) ignores real workload shifts!
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: Think of an express checkout lane sorted strictly by basket size once the cashier finishes scanning the current shopper cleanly (non-preemptive). Wait-time variance drops dramatically, while Exponential Averaging with α = 0.5 acts like a 50/50 thermostat predictor blending yesterday's reading with long-term climate. Where the analogy breaks: Non-preemptive SJF still waits if the 24 ms shopper stepped up at t = 0 before the 3 ms shopper arrived at t = 5—and an endless stream of 3-item baskets will starve a 100-item cart indefinitely!
  • Why Each Formula Exists: Swapping adjacent jobs L before S adds wait S to one job while saving wait L on the other, yielding net gain S − L < 0; the geometric decay (1 − α)k ensures recent bursts dominate while weights sum cleanly to 1.

1. SJF Principle & Proof of Optimality (§5.3.2)

More accurately called Shortest-Next-CPU-Burst Scheduling, SJF associates with each ready process the length of its next CPU burst (not its total lifetime). When the CPU becomes available, it picks the ready process with the smallest next burst. Ties are broken using FCFS order.

📜 Provable Optimality (Exchange Argument)
Suppose two processes sit ready: Pshort (burst S) and Plong (burst L > S). Placing Pshort before Plong causes Plong to wait S; placing Plong first causes Pshort to wait L. Moving a shorter process before a longer one decreases the waiting time of the short process more than it increases the waiting time of the long process (net change = S − L < 0). By repeating this swap, average waiting time reaches its global minimum among non-preemptive schedules!

Limitation: A general-purpose OS cannot know the future length of the next CPU burst! (And long CPU-bound processes can suffer starvation if short processes keep arriving). Instead, the kernel predicts the next burst using historical bursts.

2. Predicting Next CPU Burst: Exponential Averaging (§5.3.2 — [Textbook Beyond Slide 05])

τn+1 = α · tn + (1 − α) · τn where tn = actual measured length of the n-th CPU burst, τn = previous predicted value, τn+1 = predicted (n+1)-th burst, and 0 ≤ α ≤ 1.

Expanding the recurrence shows why recent observations weigh exponentially more than older ones:

τn+1 = αtn + (1−α)αtn−1 + (1−α)2αtn−2 + … + (1−α)jαtn−j + … + (1−α)n+1τ0
  • If α = 0: τn+1 = τn. Recent actual history is completely ignored; initial estimate τ0 rules forever (assumes unchanging process behavior).
  • If α = 1: τn+1 = tn. Past smoothed history is discarded; only the most recent actual burst tn counts.
  • If α = 0.5: Equal balance (50/50) between the most recent observation and all accumulated prior history—commonly chosen in textbook exams.

  • Slide 05 Ex 01 / Ex 04 (Simultaneous AT=0): For P1..P4 with BT = 6, 8, 7, 3 at AT=0, shortest-first order P4(3) → P1(6) → P3(7) → P2(8) yields | P4(0–3) | P1(3–9) | P3(9–16) | P2(16–24) | ⇒ Avg TAT = 13.0 ms, Avg WT = 7.0 ms, Throughput = 4 / 24 = 0.16 (truncated).

deck_06.html:
DECK 06 · PREEMPTIVE OPTIMAL SCHEDULING · SILBERSCHATZ §5.3.2

Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF — Preemptive SJF)

Silberschatz 10th Ed. §5.3.2 · Deck 06 Practice Scope
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Apply the exact SRTF preemption comparison rule whenever a new process arrives.
  • Track remaining CPU bursts across preemption splits (including Slide 06 Ex 02 & Ex 03) to construct accurate Gantt charts.
  • Compute CT, TAT, WT, Throughput, and Response Time (RT) for split processes (remember: WT ≠ RT under preemption!).
  • Diagnose why Slide 06 highlights Starvation of long jobs & preemption of high-priority long jobs (motivating Priority Scheduling!).
💡 Intuition-First Mental Model (Before the Formulas)
  • Naive Solutions → Visible Failure: Under non-preemptive SJF, arriving 1 ms too late forces a tiny 3 ms task to wait 23 ms behind an ongoing 24 ms task. Under SRTF, even Slide 06 Ex 03 drops Avg WT from 7.0 ms → 1.0 ms simply by pausing P1 to finish P3 in 3 ms! Yet if priority importance ignores burst length, a mission-critical 20 ms medical task gets preempted by tiny low-priority background tasks—the exact flaw that motivates Deck 07 Priority Scheduling!
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: Picture an emergency-room triage nurse: changing a long routine cast (24 min remaining) is paused immediately if a patient arrives needing a 3-minute EpiPen shot. However, if two patients have identical 4 min remaining treatment times (Burst == Remaining), you NEVER disrupt the active patient! Where the analogy breaks: Every preemption costs hardware Context Switch time—if micro-bursts preempt repeatedly by 0.5 ms margins, real wall-clock throughput drops below non-preemptive SJF.
  • Why Each Formula Exists: Comparing remaining time against arriving burst extends the optimality exchange argument across time instants; using strict < (not ≤) avoids zero-gain context switches on ties.

1. The Preemptive Decision Rule (§5.3.2)

Shortest-Remaining-Time-First (SRTF) is the preemptive counterpart to SJF. While a process runs on the CPU, a new process may arrive with a next CPU burst shorter than what the currently executing process still has left to finish.

⚠️ The Exact SRTF Preemption Test
If Burst(Pnew) < Remaining Burst(Prunning)  ⇒  PREEMPT Prunning! Strict less-than (<)! If Burst(Pnew) == Remaining(Prunning), DO NOT preempt—the running process retains the CPU (avoids pointless context switch overhead).
When preempted, the running process updates its remaining burst in its PCB, returns to the Ready Queue, and the newly arrived shorter process immediately starts.

2. Textbook Worked Example (Silberschatz 10th Ed. §5.3.2): SRTF Gantt Trace

🧮 Tick-by-Tick Execution Trace
  1. t = 0: Only P1 (BT = 8) is ready. P1 begins executing.
  2. t = 1: P2 arrives (BT = 4). P1 has run 1 ms → Remaining(P1) = 8 − 1 = 7 ms. Since 4 < 7, P1 is preempted! P2 starts.
  3. t = 2: P3 arrives (BT = 9). Remaining(P2) = 4 − 1 = 3 ms. Since 9 > 3, P2 continues.
  4. t = 3: P4 arrives (BT = 5). Remaining(P2) = 3 − 1 = 2 ms. Since 5 > 2, P2 continues.
  5. t = 5: P2 completes (CT = 5). Ready Queue: P1(rem=7), P3(9), P4(5). Shortest is P4(5) → P4 runs 5–10.
  6. t = 10: P4 completes (CT = 10). Ready Queue: P1(rem=7), P3(9). Shortest is P1(7) → P1 runs 10–17.
  7. t = 17: P1 completes (CT = 17). Remaining job P3(9) runs 17–26 (CT = 26).

3. Deck 06 Worked Example 03 & SJF vs. SRTF Trade-Offs

🧮 Slide 06 Ex 03 (P1=5,24; P2=1,3; P3=8,3) — Preemption & Idle Gaps
  • t = 0–1: CPU Idle (no arrivals yet). t = 1–4: P2 arrives & finishes uninterrupted (CT = 4). t = 4–5: CPU Idle until P1 arrives at t = 5.
  • t = 5–8: P1 runs 3 ms (Remaining(P1) = 21 ms). At t = 8, P3 arrives with BT = 3 < 21 ⇒ P1 is preempted!
  • t = 8–11: P3 finishes (CT = 11). t = 11–32: P1 resumes and finishes remaining 21 ms (CT = 32).
  • Results: Ready Queue trace = [P1, P2, P1, P3] (execution chunks); TATs = 27, 3, 3 ⇒ Avg TAT = 11.0 ms; WTs = 3, 0, 0 ⇒ Avg WT = 1.0 ms; Throughput = 3 / (32 − 1) = 0.09 (Slide 06 truncates 3/31 to 2 decimals; contrast with non-preemptive SJF Ex 03 Avg WT = 7.0 ms!). Note: when all jobs arrive at t = 0 (Slide 06 Ex 04: 6, 8, 7, 3), SRTF produces the exact same schedule as SJF (Avg WT = 7.0, TP = 0.16).

On the Silberschatz §5.3.2 4-process dataset above, non-preemptive SJF yields | P1 (0–8) | P2 (8–12) | P4 (12–17) | P3 (17–26) | with Waiting Times P1=0, P2=7, P4=9, P3=15 → Average WT = 31 / 4 = 7.75 ms (vs. 6.5 ms in SRTF!).

  • Optimality: SRTF gives the lowest mathematically possible average waiting time across all scheduling policies for any given arrival pattern.
  • Slide 06 Weaknesses & Transition: (1) Higher context-switch overhead than SJF; (2) Still requires burst-time prediction; (3) Jobs with huge bursts suffer starvation; (4) A higher-priority critical job with a big burst loses the CPU to tiny unimportant jobs—motivating Priority Scheduling (Deck 07).

deck_07.html:
DECK 07 · PRIORITY DISPATCH · SILBERSCHATZ §5.3.4

Priority Scheduling, Indefinite Starvation & The Aging Mechanism

Silberschatz 10th Ed. §5.3.4 & §5.6.3–§5.6.4 (Internal/External & RMS/EDF beyond Deck 07) · Core Topic Scope (Practice Q6)
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Apply Silberschatz / Slide 07 priority rules (lower integer = higher priority unless inverted), tie-breakers (PID in Slide 07 vs. FCFS in Mock Q6), and the Quick Guide rule: "Read the priority rule twice!"
  • Execute both Non-Preemptive and Preemptive Priority Gantt charts + Ready Queues (Slide 07 Ex 03 & Mock Midterm Q6) and spot the Ex 03 erratum.
  • Diagnose Indefinite Blocking (Starvation) and prevent it using Aging (§5.3.4).
  • Compare Internal vs. External priorities (§5.3.4), Priority + Round Robin (§5.3.4), and Real-Time Scheduling (RMS §5.6.3 & EDF §5.6.4) [Textbook Beyond Slide 07].
💡 Intuition-First Mental Model (Before the Formulas)
  • Naive Solutions → Visible Failure: Letting strictly static priorities rule without escalation means a continuous stream of Priority-1 jobs leaves a Priority-127 maintenance job stranded for years (the real MIT IBM 7094 shutdown story: a 1967 job still sitting unrun in 1973!).
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: Imagine a hospital triage board with an auto-escalator clock: critical cases jump straight to the front, while anyone waiting patiently has their urgency ticket bumped closer to Priority 0 every tick (Aging) so nobody dies waiting in the hallway. Where the analogy breaks: Unlike human queues, OS scheduling exams flip conventions on purpose—some problems state "larger number = higher priority" and tie-break rules flip between PID (Slide 07) and FCFS (Mock Midterm Q6)!
  • Why Each Formula Exists: Decreasing integer rank linearly with ⌊Wait / Interval⌋ bounds worst-case starvation latency mathematically (from 127 to 0 in ~127 s ≈ 2 min at 1 boost/sec); Real-Time EDF sorts dynamically by deadline because static RMS leaves ~31% headroom stranded at high utilization.

1. Priority Scheduling Principles & Exam Rules (§5.3.4)

A priority integer is attached to every process PCB, and the CPU goes to the ready process holding the highest priority. Notice that SJF is simply a special case of Priority Scheduling where priority is inversely proportional to predicted next CPU burst (priority ∝ 1 / τn+1). [Textbook Beyond Slide 07]: Priorities can be Internal (time limits, memory, open files, avg I/O burst / avg CPU burst ratio) or External (user importance, funds paid, politics).

⚠️ Exam Conventions: "Read the Priority Rule Twice!"
  • Direction Trap: In Silberschatz 10th Ed. and CPCS-361 Slide 07, smaller number = higher priority (1 > 2 > 3)—UNLESS the question explicitly inverts it (e.g., "higher number = higher priority"!). Always verify before tracing!
  • Tie-Breaker Difference: Slide 07 (P6) specifies that when Arrival Time and Priority are both equal, break ties by smaller Process Identifier (PID); however, the Practice Exam Q6 convention explicitly uses FCFS (earlier arrival)—and remember to draw the Ready Queue (0.5 marks)!
  • Non-Preemptive Priority: Simply places the arriving higher-priority process at the head of the ready queue; waits until the current process yields or finishes.
  • Preemptive Priority: Immediately preempts the running process if a newly arriving process has strictly higher priority (smaller priority integer). Equal priorities do not preempt.
  • Priority with Round Robin (§5.3.4): Runs highest-priority processes until higher priorities finish, and schedules multiple processes at the exact same priority level using Round Robin (time-sliced with quantum q) so peers share the CPU fairly.

2. Indefinite Blocking (Starvation) & Aging (§5.3.4)

Starvation (Indefinite Blocking): A ready low-priority process can sit waiting forever if a continuous stream of higher-priority processes keeps arriving. Famous textbook anecdote: when MIT's IBM 7094 shut down in 1973, engineers found a low-priority process submitted in 1967 that had still not executed after 6 years!

📜 Textbook Solution: Aging (Silberschatz 10th Ed. §5.3.4)
"Aging involves gradually increasing the priority of processes that wait in the system for a long time."
Priority(t) = max(TopPriority,  InitialPriority − ⌊WaitingTime / AgingInterval⌋) Silberschatz 10th Ed. Example: Priorities 127 (lowest) to 0 (highest). Periodically (say, every second) increasing waiting priority by 1 takes a little over 2 minutes (~127 s) for a priority-127 job to age to priority 0, guaranteeing execution!

4. Extension: Real-Time Priority Scheduling (§5.6.3–§5.6.4 — [Textbook Beyond Slide 07])

  • Rate-Monotonic Scheduling (RMS — §5.6.3): Assigns static priorities inversely proportional to task period p (shorter period = higher priority). Optimal among fixed-priority policies, bounded CPU utilization ~69% for large N.
  • Earliest-Deadline-First (EDF — §5.6.4): Assigns dynamic priorities according to closest upcoming deadline. Theoretically optimal—can achieve up to 100% CPU utilization while still meeting every hard deadline!

deck_08.html:
DECK 08 · TIME-SHARING & MULTILEVEL DISPATCH · SILBERSCHATZ §5.3.3–§5.5

Round Robin (RR), Time Quantum Sizing, MLQ, MLFQ & Multiprocessor Scheduling

Silberschatz 10th Ed. §5.3.3, §5.3.5, §5.3.6 & §5.5 (Multiprocessor §5.5 beyond Deck 08) · Deck 08 Practice Scope
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Trace circular FIFO ready-queue preemption under Round Robin (RR) scheduling, including Slide 08 Ex 02's subtle arrival-before-requeue race (§5.3.3).
  • Evaluate how Time Quantum (q) size impacts context-switch overhead, responsiveness, and Turnaround Time (Silberschatz Fig. 5.6).
  • Compare fixed-partition Multilevel Queue (MLQ) against adaptive Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ) (§5.3.5–§5.3.6).
  • List all MLFQ defining parameters (Slide 08's 4 parameters + last queue always FCFS, vs. Silberschatz §5.3.6's 5 parameters).
  • Explain Processor Affinity (Soft vs. Hard, NUMA) and Load Balancing (Push vs. Pull Migration) on multicore CPUs [Textbook §5.5 Beyond Slide 08].
💡 Intuition-First Mental Model (Before the Formulas)
  • Naive Solutions → Visible Failure: Letting quantum q = 1,000 ms collapses right back into FCFS's Convoy Effect; shrinking q = 1 ms when a context switch itself costs 1 ms burns 50% of all CPU electricity just shuffling registers! Even worse, assuming a larger q always reduces Avg TAT fails empirically (Fig. 5.6) whenever splitting pushes multiple nearly-done jobs just past a cycle!
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: Think of speed chess with a shared timer + a multi-tier DMV. In Round Robin, everyone gets an equal q = 4 ms turn before cycling to the back of the line (max wait per round = (n − 1) q); in MLFQ, newcomers start at express Desk Q0 (8 ms), spill-overs drop to Q1 (16 ms), and heavy batch jobs land at slow Q2 (FCFS). Where the analogy breaks: On multicore hardware, keeping a process on its original desk keeps its L1/L2 CPU cache warm (Processor Affinity), so over-aggressive Load Balancing that moves threads between cores actually slows memory access down—especially across remote NUMA sockets!
  • Why Each Formula Exists: Setting q so ~80% of bursts finish inside 1 slice gives sub-quantum responsiveness while avoiding repeated context switches; Push/Pull migration balances per-core queues when affinity isn't hard-pinned.

1. Round Robin (RR) Algorithm (§5.3.3)

Designed specifically for time-sharing interactive systems, Round Robin behaves like FCFS plus hardware-timer preemption using a small fixed unit of time called a Time Quantum (q) (typically 10–100 ms):

  1. The Ready Queue operates as a circular FIFO queue; newly arriving processes join its tail.
  2. Scheduler pops the head process, sets the timer interrupt for 1 quantum = q, and dispatches the process.
  3. Two outcomes occur:
    • Burst ≤ q: The process voluntarily releases the CPU (finishes or blocks on I/O) before timer expiry; scheduler immediately dispatches the next ready process.
    • Burst > q: Timer fires at q, interrupts the process, context switches, and places the preempted process at the tail of the Ready Queue.

2. Critical Impact of Time Quantum q Size

Quantum SettingSystem BehaviorExam Takeaway
q → ∞ (Extremely Large)No timer interrupts ever fire before processes finish or block.Degenerates strictly into FCFS (reintroducing the Convoy Effect!).
q → 0 (Extremely Small)Creates illusion of Processor Sharing where each of N processes thinks it owns a private CPU at 1/N speed—but Context Switch Overhead dominates!If q = 1 ms and context switch = 1 ms, 50% of CPU power is wasted switching!
Optimal Tuningq must be much larger than context-switch time (CS < 10 μs vs q = 10–100 ms).80% Rule of Thumb: About 80% of CPU bursts should be shorter than q so short jobs finish within 1 turn.

Subtle Exam Trap (Silberschatz Fig. 5.6 — How Turnaround Time Varies with q): Average Turnaround Time under RR does not necessarily improve monotonically as q increases! Decreasing q lowers TAT for some sets and raises it for others whenever extra splits prolong completion beyond q (a famous rule of thumb puts 80% of CPU bursts shorter than q).

3. Slide 08 Worked Examples: Round Robin (q = 4 ms)

🧮 Slide 08 Ex 01 (AT=0) & Ex 02 (Staggered Enqueue Race Trap!)

Ex 01 (P1=24, P2=3, P3=3; AT=0, q=4):

Gantt Chart (Draw separate 4 ms slices on exams!): | P1 (0–4) | P2 (4–7) | P3 (7–10) | P1 (10–14) | P1 (14–18) | P1 (18–22) | P1 (22–26) | P1 (26–30) |

ProcessBTCTTAT (CT − AT)WT (TAT − BT)RT (First Start − AT)
P124 ms30 ms30 − 0 = 30 ms30 − 24 = 6 ms0 ms
P23 ms7 ms7 − 0 = 7 ms7 − 3 = 4 ms4 ms
P33 ms10 ms10 − 0 = 10 ms10 − 3 = 7 ms7 ms

Ex 01 Averages: Avg TAT = 47 / 3 = 15.67 ms (Slide truncates to 15.6), Avg WT = 17 / 3 = 5.67 ms (Slide truncates to 5.6), Throughput = 0.10. Notice this worked trace explicitly draws each q=4 turn of P1 individually (10–14, 14–18, 18–22, 22–26, 26–30) and puts every occurrence in the Ready Queue!

Ex 02 (Crucial Enqueue Ordering Trap — P1(AT=2, BT=24), P2(15, 6), P3(5, 3); q=4):

  • 0–2: CPU Idle. 2–6: P1 runs first slice (20 left). Meanwhile at t = 5, P3 arrives first → P3 joins Ready Queue ahead of preempted P1 arriving back at t = 6 (Queue: P3, P1)!
  • 6–9: P3 runs 3 ms and finishes early (CT = 9, TAT = 4, WT = 1).
  • 9–17: P1 runs two slices (9–13 and 13–17; 12 ms left). While P1 runs 13–17, P2 arrives at t = 15, entering the Ready Queue before P1 expires at t = 17!
  • 17–21: P2 runs its first 4 ms slice (2 ms left) → re-queues behind P1 at t = 21. Remaining trace: P1(21–25) | P2(25–27, CT=27) | P1(27–31) | P1(31–35, CT=35)!
  • Ex 02 Results: Slide Ready Queue trace = [P1, P3, P1, P2, P1, P2, P1...] (dispatch sequence), CTs = (35, 27, 9), Avg TAT = (33+12+4)/3 = 16.3, Avg WT = (9+6+1)/3 = 5.3, Throughput = 3 / (35 − 2) = 0.09!

4. Multilevel Queue (MLQ) vs. Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ)

Multilevel Queue (MLQ — §5.3.5)

Ready queue is statically partitioned into distinct priority queues (e.g., Real-time > System > Interactive > Batch). Each queue runs its own algorithm (e.g., RR for Interactive, FCFS for Batch). Between queues: fixed-priority preemptive scheduling or time slicing (e.g., 80% foreground / 20% background).
Flaw: Processes are locked permanently in their assigned queue → low-priority queues can starve.

Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ — §5.3.6)

Processes dynamically migrate between queues based on runtime behavior!
• Uses too much CPU time (hits full quantum) → Demoted to a lower-priority queue.
• Waits too long in a low queue → Promoted (Aging) upward to prevent starvation.
Genius Effect: Interactive & I/O-bound tasks stay near the top with tiny latency while long CPU hogs sink naturally.

⚠️ Memorize All MLFQ Parameters (Silberschatz §5.3.6 vs. Slide 08)
  1. The number of queues (e.g., Q0, Q1, Q2).
  2. The scheduling algorithm for each queue (e.g., Q0: RR q=8; Q1: RR q=16; Q2: FCFS).
  3. The rule determining when to upgrade (promote) a process to a higher-priority queue.
  4. The rule determining when to demote a process to a lower-priority queue (explicitly listed as #4 in Silberschatz §5.3.6; baked into per-queue quantum expiry on Slide 08).
  5. The rule determining which queue a process enters initially when it needs service.

Slide 08 Crucial Exam Rule (P106): Except the last queue, every queue has its own time quantum; the last (lowest-priority) queue ALWAYS uses FCFS!

5. Multi-Processor Scheduling, Affinity & Load Balancing (§5.5 — [Textbook Beyond Slide 08])

  • Processor Affinity: Running a thread on the same core keeps its cache ("warm cache") valid. Soft affinity: OS attempts to keep the process on the same core, no guarantee. Hard affinity: OS allows explicit syscall pinning (sched_setaffinity() on Linux) to specific core IDs. Coupled with NUMA, scheduler tries to allocate memory on the local socket.
  • Load Balancing: Keeps workload distributed across SMP cores (only needed when each core keeps a private ready queue): Push migration uses a periodic kernel task to move excess processes from busy to idle cores; Pull migration lets an idle core steal a waiting task from an overloaded neighbor. Note: load balancing directly opposes cache affinity!

deck_09.html:
DECK 09 · CONCURRENCY HAZARDS · SILBERSCHATZ §3.5 & CH. 6

Process Synchronization: Race Conditions, Machine Disassembly & Bounded Buffer

Silberschatz 10th Ed. §3.5, §6.1–§6.2 · Core Topic Scope (Practice Q3)
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Understand cooperating processes sharing memory or kernel structures and define a Race Condition formally (§6.1).
  • Disassemble C statements count++ and count-- into 3 machine instructions and trace corrupted interleavings.
  • Identify real OS kernel race conditions (e.g., fork() assigning duplicate PIDs on next_available_pid, §6.2 Fig. 6.2).
  • Distinguish Non-Preemptive Kernels vs. Preemptive Kernels in handling kernel-mode races (§6.2).
  • Trace and write every line of the Bounded-Buffer Producer/Consumer code (§3.5 & Mock Midterm Q3), plus the counter trade-off (§6.1 / Slide 09).
💡 Intuition First: Why One C Line Splits Into a Concurrency Trap
  • Naive Attempt → Visible Failure: A lock-free ring buffer wastes 1 slot (BUFFER_SIZE − 1) because otherwise in == out could mean either Empty or Full. Trying to reclaim that lost slot by adding a shared integer counter (counter++ / counter--) fails under preemption: if CPU timer interrupts hit mid-update, both counter = 4 and counter = 6 can overwrite the true 5!
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: Picture two accountants updating one shared chalkboard balance (count = 5) using private scratchpads (register1, register2): Clerk A writes 5 + 1 = 6 on his pad, steps out, Clerk B reads 5, writes 4 to the board, and Clerk A returns to overwrite 4 with 6. Where the analogy breaks: Unlike human clerks, CPU cores save and restore each thread's private scratchpad inside its PCB across interrupts (§6.1), so neither process has any clue the chalkboard changed while it was swapped out!
  • Why Each Rule Exists: Leaving one sentinel empty cell in ((in + 1) % N) == out avoids touching any shared counter at all; Preemptive kernels still need locks on next_available_pid because kernel preemption and SMP multi-core execution interleave kernel assembly instructions just like user threads.

1. Background & Formal Definition of a Race Condition (§6.1)

A cooperating process can affect or be affected by other processes executing concurrently (via shared logical address space, threads, or shared files). When multiple execution flows access shared mutable data without coordination, memory consistency breaks down unpredictably depending on the exact nanosecond timing of timer interrupts or multicore bus arbitration.

📜 Textbook Definition: Race Condition (Silberschatz §6.1)
"A situation where several processes access and manipulate the same data concurrently and the outcome of the execution depends on the particular order in which the access takes place, is called a race condition."

Real Kernel Race Condition (§6.2, Fig. 6.2): Inside an OS kernel, two processes simultaneously calling fork() might both read the same integer next_available_pid = 2615 before either increments it—causing the kernel to assign two completely distinct child processes the exact same PID! Other kernel targets include open-file tables, memory allocation bitmaps, and ready queues.

2. Dissecting count++ and count-- at Assembly Level

Wait—isn't count++ a single statement in C? Not to the CPU! A load-store architecture compiles count++ and count-- into 3 separate machine instructions each:

Producer: count++

P1: LOAD  register1, count
P2: ADD   register1, #1
P3: STORE count, register1

Consumer: count--

C1: LOAD  register2, count
C2: SUB   register2, #1
C3: STORE count, register2
🧮 Interleaving Trace: Initially count = 5 (Why Outcome Becomes 4, 5, or 6!)

Logically, running 1 increment and 1 decrement should leave count == 5. Yet look at this interleaved trace across context switches:

StepActorMachine Instruction Executedregister1register2Memory count
T0Producerregister1 = count5—5
T1Producerregister1 = register1 + 16—5
T2Consumerregister2 = count (context switch!)655
T3Consumerregister2 = register2 − 1645
T4Producercount = register1646
T5Consumercount = register2 (OVERWRITES 6!)644

If T4 and T5 execute in reverse order, final count = 6. Only non-overlapping execution leaves count = 5. Every outcome (4, 5, or 6) is possible depending solely on instruction timing!

3. Non-Preemptive vs. Preemptive Kernels (§6.2)

  • Non-Preemptive Kernel: A kernel-mode process runs until it exits kernel mode, blocks, or voluntarily yields. Essentially free from kernel data-structure race conditions on a single CPU, since at most one process executes inside kernel code at once.
  • Preemptive Kernel (Linux, Windows, Solaris): Allows a process running in kernel mode to be preempted. Requires careful mutex/spinlock synchronization inside kernel paths, but provides far better responsiveness (real-time processes don't stall behind long syscalls) and works naturally on SMP multicore CPUs where two cores execute kernel code simultaneously anyway.

4. The Bounded-Buffer Shared-Memory Trace (§3.5 & Mock Midterm Q3)

Consider the circular shared buffer of size BUFFER_SIZE from Silberschatz §3.5 (note: Lecture Slide 09 traces BUFFER_SIZE = 6 with indices 0..5, showing Producer stalled at in=5, out=0 because (5+1)%6 == 0, and then motivates adding an integer counter initialized at 3 that races to 2 or 4!). Why does this lock-free design leave 1 slot unused (maximum BUFFER_SIZE − 1 items)? If it allowed filling all N slots, in == out would ambiguously mean both Empty and Full—whereas using counter == BUFFER_SIZE uses all N slots at the price of a shared-counter race condition unless synchronized!

#define BUFFER_SIZE 10
typedef struct { ... } item;
item buffer[BUFFER_SIZE];
int in = 0;   // next free slot to write
int out = 0;  // first full slot to read

Producer Process (Mock Midterm Q3.B)

while (true) {
    /* produce item in next_produced */
    while (((in + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE) == out)
        ; /* do nothing -- buffer full */
    buffer[in] = next_produced;
    in = (in + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
}

Consumer Process (Mock Midterm Q3.A)

while (true) {
    while (in == out)
        ; /* do nothing -- buffer empty */
    next_consumed = buffer[out];
    out = (out + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
    /* consume item in next_consumed */
}
⚠️ Mock Midterm Question 3 Full-Marks Checklist
  • Purpose of while (in == out);: Busy-waits (blocks) the consumer whenever the shared buffer is empty, preventing it from reading stale or uninitialized memory.
  • Purpose of % BUFFER_SIZE: Implements a circular ring buffer; when in or out increments past index BUFFER_SIZE − 1 (9), modulo arithmetic wraps it cleanly back to 0 to reuse consumed slots without copying/shifting array elements.
  • Modifying for an Unbounded Buffer (Q3.C): (1) Delete the producer's buffer-full busy-wait loop while (((in + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE) == out); since infinite capacity never fills; (2) Remove % BUFFER_SIZE, turning updates into in = in + 1; and out = out + 1; (or arbitrary unbounded queue pointers). Note: consumer still keeps empty-check loop!

deck_10.html:
DECK 10 · SYNCHRONIZATION ALGORITHMS · SILBERSCHATZ §6.2–§6.5

The Critical-Section Problem, Peterson's Solution, Memory Barriers & Hardware Atomics

Silberschatz 10th Ed. Chapter 6 (§6.2–§6.5) · Core Topic Scope (Practice Q4)
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Identify all 4 Code Sections of a concurrent process: Entry, Critical, Exit, and Remainder (§6.2).
  • State and evaluate the 3 Cardinal Requirements: Mutual Exclusion, Progress, and Bounded Waiting.
  • Diagnose why Software Attempt 1 (turn variable) fails Progress (Mock Midterm Q4.A).
  • Trace Peterson's Solution step-by-step, prove all 3 requirements, and explain its modern Memory Barrier limitation (Mock Midterm Q4.B, §6.3–§6.4).
  • Write mutex algorithms using hardware atomics: test_and_set() / Swap() / compare_and_swap() (including waiting[n] Bounded Waiting) and understand atomic-integer caveats (§6.4).
  • Distinguish blocking Mutexes vs. Spinlocks and the 2 context switches rule (§6.5).
💡 Intuition First: Two Polite Engineers & Why Hardware Reordering Cheats
  • Naive Attempts → Visible Failure: Attempt 1 (turn = j) guarantees Mutual Exclusion yet violates Progress—if your partner goes to sleep outside the room, the lock stays permanently jammed on their turn. Pure flag-checking without turn deadlocks when both raise flags simultaneously. Even naive while (TestAndSet(&lock)); satisfies Mutual Exclusion + Progress yet lacks Bounded Waiting if one fast core repeatedly grabs the lock before slower cores win arbitration!
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: Peterson's algorithm is two polite engineers sharing a 1-person server closet: each first posts an "I want in" sticky note on their own door (flag[i] = true), then writes "After you" on the hallway whiteboard (turn = j). Since only the second writer's name stays on the whiteboard, the earlier writer walks straight in while the later writer waits. Where the analogy breaks: On modern multi-core CPUs, private store buffers let your turn = j whiteboard write become visible to the other core before your flag[i] = true sticky note flushes from cache—letting both walk inside together unless a Memory Barrier flushes writes (§6.4.1)!
  • Why Each Rule Exists: Why turn = j MUST follow flag[i] = true (prevents P1 from observing flag[0] == false after P0 already yielded); why Spinlocks follow the < 2 context switches rule (blocking costs both a save-to-wait switch and a wakeup-to-ready switch; only busy-wait when the holder will release sooner on another core).

1. Structure & Three Cardinal Requirements (§6.2)

Consider n concurrent processes {P0, P1, …, Pn−1}. Each process contains a Critical Section (CS) accessing shared variables. Permission to enter must be requested in the Entry Section, released in the Exit Section, and independent work runs in the Remainder Section.

RequirementExact Textbook Meaning (§6.2)What Breaks When Violated?
1. Mutual ExclusionIf process Pi is executing inside its critical section, no other processes can execute inside their critical sections simultaneously.Data corruption / race conditions on shared state.
2. ProgressIf no process is in its CS and some wish to enter, only processes not in their Remainder Section can participate in deciding who enters next, and this selection cannot be postponed indefinitely.Deadlock or artificial blocking by an idle outside process (strict alternation trap!).
3. Bounded WaitingThere exists a limit (bound) on the number of times other processes are allowed to enter their CS after Pi has made a request and before that request is granted.Starvation (indefinite postponement) of Pi.

2. Software Attempt 1: Single turn Variable (Mock Midterm Q4.A)

// Process Pi (with peer Pj, j = 1 - i)
do {
    while (turn != i) ;  // Entry Section (Mock Q4.A writes: while (turn == j); )
        /* critical section */
    turn = j;            // Exit Section
        /* remainder section */
} while (true);

Exam Analysis: Does it satisfy Mutual Exclusion? YES (turn holds either 0 or 1, never both). Does it satisfy Progress? NO! Suppose turn = 0 and P0 is sleeping forever in its Remainder Section (doesn't need CS), while P1 desperately wants to enter. P1 spins forever waiting for P0 to finish and set turn = 1! Because a process in its Remainder Section blocks P1, strict alternation violates Progress. (Notation note: Mock Midterm Q4.A writes while (turn == j); starting at turn = 1 with P0 requesting first—exact same logic, P0 stalls!)

3. Peterson's 2-Process Solution (Mock Midterm Q4.B, §6.3)

Peterson combines two shared variables: boolean flag[2] = {false, false}; (intent to enter) and int turn; (courteous tie-breaker).

// Process Pi (peer Pj = 1 - i)
do {
    flag[i] = true;                // 1. Declare MY intent to enter
    turn = j;                      // 2. Politely give turn to the OTHER process
    while (flag[j] && turn == j) ; // 3. Wait ONLY if other wants in AND it's their turn
        /* critical section */
    flag[i] = false;               // 4. Clear intent on exit
        /* remainder section */
} while (true);
🧮 Trace Exam Question: P0 writes flag[0]=true, then P1 sets flag[1]=true, P0 sets turn=1, then P1 sets turn=0
Step / Stateflag[0]flag[1]turnSpin Condition Evaluation
Initialfalsefalse—Neither process requesting
P0: flag[0]=true; P1: flag[1]=truetruetrue—Both declare intent
P0: turn = 1truetrue1P0 yields to P1
P1: turn = 0 (overwrites!)truetrue0Final value of turn is 0!
Loop Evaluationtruetrue0• P0 checks: flag[1] && turn==1 → true && false → FALSE ⇒ P0 ENTERS CS!
• P1 checks: flag[0] && turn==0 → true && true → TRUE ⇒ P1 WAITS!

Proof Sketch for All 3 Criteria: (1) Mutual Exclusion: Both enter CS only if flag[0]==flag[1]==true AND simultaneously turn==0 and turn==1—impossible! (2) Progress & Bounded Waiting: If P1 exits CS, it sets flag[1]=false allowing P0 in; even if P1 immediately loops back and tries again, P1 sets turn=0, forcing itself to wait and guaranteeing P0 waits at most 1 entry!

Silberschatz 10th Ed. Caveat (§6.3–§6.4.1): In a Strongly Ordered memory model, memory modifications on one processor are immediately visible to all other processors; in a Weakly Ordered model (modern x86/ARM out-of-order CPUs and optimizing compilers), independent writes like flag[i] = true; turn = j; may be reordered unless protected by explicit Memory Barriers (memory_barrier()) that flush write buffers. Exam Note: Slide 10 (slide 102) remarks informally that Peterson can starve, whereas Silberschatz §6.3 formally proves Bounded Waiting (max 1 turn wait on sequentially consistent hardware); its real limits are 2-process scope, busy-waiting, and weak memory ordering.

4. Hardware Synchronization & Atomics (§6.4)

Disabling interrupts (CLI/STI) prevents context switches on a uniprocessor, but fails to scale on multi-core CPUs (sending IPIs across 64 cores kills throughput and skews system clocks). Instead, modern hardware provides uninterruptible (atomic) instructions (Silberschatz 10th Ed. names these lowercase test_and_set / compare_and_swap; Slide 10 also covers 2-process Swap(&a, &b) and n-process TestAndSet with waiting[n]):

TestAndSet (&target)

boolean TestAndSet(boolean *target) {
    boolean rv = *target;
    *target = true;
    return rv;
}
// Mutex usage:
while (TestAndSet(&lock)) ; // spin
    /* critical section */
lock = false;

Flaw: Naive loop guarantees Mutual Exclusion & Progress, NOT Bounded Waiting (one lucky core can keep grabbing lock!). Adding a circular waiting[n] scan grants Bounded Waiting.

Edition Note: Silberschatz 10th Ed. Fig. 6.9 implements circular waiting[n] Bounded Waiting using compare_and_swap(&lock, 0, 1) (9th Ed. and Slide 10 showed the same waiting[n] scan with TestAndSet).

CompareAndSwap (&val, exp, new)

int CompareAndSwap(int *v, int exp, int nw) {
    int temp = *v;
    if (*v == exp)
        *v = nw;
    return temp;
}
// Mutex usage (0=unlocked, 1=locked):
while (CompareAndSwap(&lock, 0, 1) != 0) ;
    /* critical section */
lock = 0;

Also powers lock-free Atomic Variables (e.g., increment(&v) via CAS retry loop, §6.4.3). Crucial Caveat: Atomic integers protect single-variable increments, NOT multi-step invariants like two consumers both checking count > 0 simultaneously when count == 1!

5. Mutex Locks & Spinlocks (§6.5)

An OS Mutex Lock exposes acquire() and release() around critical sections using an atomic available boolean. Notice lock contention occurs whenever a thread blocks/spins waiting on a held mutex. When implemented via busy waiting (spinning in a loop), it is called a Spinlock.

  • When Spinlocks Win (Multi-Core + "Short Duration" Hold): Zero context-switch overhead! Silberschatz §6.5 formally defines a short lock duration as less than two context switches (~1–5 μs): spinning on Core B while Core A finishes beats sleeping and waking up.
  • When Spinlocks Fail (Single-Core!): On a 1-core CPU, the spinning process burns its entire remaining time quantum stopping the lock holder from even running to call release()!

  • Master Monitors & Condition Variables (x.wait(), x.signal()) and Signal-and-Wait vs. Signal-and-Continue semantics (§6.7, textbook extension beyond Slide 11).
💡 Intuition First: Parking Garage Gates, Shop Bells & The Ambulance Tunnel
  • Naive Attempts → Visible Failure: Busy-waiting while (S ≤ 0); stalls a 1-core CPU until its quantum expires (§6.6.2). Switching to sleep()/block() stops CPU waste, yet writing wait(mutex); wait(empty); in Producer-Consumer deadlocks the moment the buffer fills (empty == 0): Producer sleeps holding mutex, so Consumer can never enter to drain an item and call signal(empty)!
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: Counting Semaphores are parking garage entry/exit gates tracking two live tallies (empty open bays, full parked cars) plus a 1-key booth mutex; negative S->value = −3 means 3 cars queued in the waiting lane. Where the analogy breaks (Semaphore vs. Monitor Condition Variable): A Semaphore remembers every past signal() inside its integer counter (S->value++), whereas a Monitor's x.signal() (§6.7.1) is a shop counter bell—if nobody is standing at the bell, the ring vanishes completely! And Priority Inversion (§6.8.2) is an express ambulance (H) trapped behind a slow truck (L) in a 1-lane tunnel while endless commuter cars (M) cut off L's CPU time—until Priority Inheritance puts an ambulance siren on L.
  • Why Each Rule Exists: Why S->value-- runs before testing S->value < 0 (§6.6.2: keeps |S->value| equal to exact sleeping queue size); why availability waits (empty/full) MUST wrap outside mutex.

1. Semaphores & Non-Busy-Waiting Queues (§6.6)

A Semaphore S (introduced by Edsger Dijkstra: P = proberen "test" / wait, V = verhogen "increment" / signal) is an integer variable accessed strictly through initialization and two atomic operations:

  • Binary Semaphore: Value ranges only over {0, 1}—equivalent in function to a mutex lock.
  • Counting Semaphore: Value ranges over an unrestricted integer domain—controls access to a resource pool with K identical instances (initialized to K) or enforces ordering constraints (S = 0 so T2 waits for signal(S) from T1).
typedef struct {
    int value;
    struct process *list; // Waiting PCB queue
} semaphore;

void wait(semaphore *S) {
    S->value--;
    if (S->value < 0) {
        add this process to S->list;
        block();   // Moves caller to Waiting state (Silberschatz 10th Ed. names this sleep())
    }
}

void signal(semaphore *S) {
    S->value++;
    if (S->value <= 0) {
        remove a process P from S->list;
        wakeup(P); // Moves P from Waiting → Ready queue
    }
}
⚠️ Crucial Exam Property: Negative Semaphore Magnitude
In the block/wakeup implementation above (Slide 11 calls it block(); Silberschatz §6.6.2 calls it sleep()), S->value CAN become negative! When S->value < 0, its absolute value |S->value| equals the exact number of processes currently asleep on S->list. For instance, if S starts at 2 and 5 threads execute wait(S), final S->value = -3, meaning 3 threads are blocked waiting on S. (Note: Slide 11 also demonstrates pthread_mutex_t in C with two threads incrementing a counter 100,000 times and traces a 6-slot bounded buffer starting mid-run at mutex=1, empty=3, full=3.)

2. Deadlock & Priority Inversion Pitfalls (§6.8.1–§6.8.2, §6.9 & Mock Midterm Q5)

Crossed Wait Deadlock (§6.8.1 & Mock Q5)

// Initial: S = 1, Q = 1
Thread T1:        Thread T2:
wait(S);          wait(Q);
wait(Q);          wait(S); // DEADLOCK!

Trace: T1 grabs S (S=0), context switch → T2 grabs Q (Q=0). Now T1 blocks on wait(Q) while holding S, and T2 blocks on wait(S) while holding Q! Mock Q5.A Print Test: "12", "21", or nothing (deadlock) are possible; only "1" is IMPOSSIBLE because once T1 finishes printing it immediately signals both locks so T2 finishes! Fix: Enforce canonical resource ordering—make both T1 and T2 execute wait(S) before wait(Q).

Priority Inversion & Inheritance (§6.8.2 & §6.9)

Low-priority process L holds lock R needed by high-priority process H. Medium-priority process M (needing no lock) preempts L, delaying L indefinitely and indirectly starving H! (Famously reset NASA's Mars Pathfinder, §6.9 box!).
Fix — Priority Inheritance Protocol (§6.8.2): Temporarily elevate L's priority to H's priority until L releases lock R.

3. Bounded-Buffer Solution Using Semaphores (§7.1.1)

We initialize three semaphores: mutex = 1 (mutual exclusion on buffer array), empty = N (counts free buffer slots), full = 0 (counts filled buffer slots).

Producer Process

while (true) {
    /* produce item in next_produced */
    wait(empty);   // 1. Reserve an empty slot
    wait(mutex);   // 2. Enter critical section

    /* add next_produced to buffer */

    signal(mutex); // 3. Leave critical section
    signal(full);  // 4. Announce +1 full item
}

Consumer Process

while (true) {
    wait(full);    // 1. Wait for a full item
    wait(mutex);   // 2. Enter critical section

    /* remove item from buffer */

    signal(mutex); // 3. Leave critical section
    signal(empty); // 4. Announce +1 free slot
    /* consume item in next_consumed */
}

Order Trap: If Producer swapped the first two lines to wait(mutex); wait(empty); while buffer is full (empty == 0), Producer acquires mutex and goes to sleep on empty; Consumer then tries wait(mutex) to drain the buffer and blocks forever → Instant Deadlock! Always acquire resource-counting semaphores before mutual-exclusion locks.

4. Monitors & Condition Variables (Silberschatz §6.7 — Textbook Beyond Slides)

Because forgetting a single signal() or swapping two wait() calls corrupts semaphores silently, compilers provide a high-level construct called a Monitor: an abstract data type encapsulating private shared data plus public procedures such that only one process can be active inside the monitor at any time. (Scope note: Slide 11 focuses on Semaphores; Monitors are full Silberschatz §6.7 textbook coverage.)

  • Condition Variables (condition x, y;): Support two operations inside a monitor:
    • x.wait(): Suspends the calling process on queue x and automatically releases the monitor lock until another process invokes x.signal().
    • x.signal(): Resumes exactly one suspended process on x. Crucial Contrast vs. Semaphores: If no process is waiting on x, x.signal() does nothing (signal is lost!), whereas semaphore signal(S) always increments S.value for future arrivals!
  • Signal-and-Wait vs. Signal-and-Continue (§6.7.1) when P executes x.signal() waking Q:
    • Signal and Wait (Hoare, §6.7.2): Signaling process P waits until Q leaves the monitor or waits for another condition (condition still holds when Q resumes).
    • Signal and Continue (commonly called Mesa semantics in POSIX/Java): Q waits until P leaves the monitor—so the guarded condition may no longer hold when Q runs, making a while (!cond) x.wait(); re-check essential!
