deck_12.html:
DECK 12 · CLASSIC SYNCHRONIZATION PROBLEMS · SILBERSCHATZ §7.1.2–§7.1.3

The Readers-Writers & Dining Philosophers Problems (Full Textbook Analysis)

Silberschatz 10th Ed. Chapter 7 (§7.1.2–§7.1.3) · Midterm & Final Exam Scope
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Formulate the synchronization constraints of shared database access in the Readers-Writers Problem (§7.1.2).
  • Trace the First Readers-Writers Algorithm line by line and prove why only the 1st and last reader touch rw_mutex.
  • Compare First (Reader-priority → Writer starvation) vs. Second (Writer-priority → Reader starvation) vs. Starvation-Free Reader-Writer Locks.
  • Prove how naive Dining Philosophers deadlocks via simultaneous left-chopstick acquisition (§7.1.3).
  • Master all 3 Semaphore deadlock remedies (§7.1.3.1, covered in Slide 12) plus Silberschatz's Monitor Solution (§7.1.3.2 — deadlock-free, though starvation remains possible!).
💡 Intuition First: The Museum Guest Clipboard & Why Deadlock-Free ≠ Starvation-Free
  • Naive Attempts → Visible Failure: Locking rw_mutex on every single reader destroys concurrent reading throughput; letting subsequent readers skip waiting once read_count > 0 lets a steady relay of incoming readers starve waiting writers (First R-W). In Dining Philosophers, initializing chopstick[5] = {1..1} with naive "left then right" freezes all 5 in circular wait!
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: Readers-Writers is a museum gallery with a guest sign-in clipboard (mutex guards read_count): the very first visitor flips the front sign to "Closed for Maintenance" (wait(rw_mutex)), all arriving guests enter together, and only the very last guest leaving flips the sign back (signal(rw_mutex)). Dining Philosophers Monitor (§7.1.3.2) puts a smart waiter in charge of chopsticks—where the intuition breaks: eliminating deadlock does NOT eliminate starvation! Even in the Monitor solution, two neighbors P0 and P2 can alternate eating shifts forever while P1 sits permanently HUNGRY (§7.1.3.2!).
  • Why Each Formula Exists: Asymmetric Odd/Even pickup ensures every adjacent odd/even pair competes for the same first chopstick instead of chasing tails (Convention note: Silberschatz treats chopstick[i] as left, whereas Slide 12's asymmetric diagram numbers chopstick[i] as right—both break the circle!); (i + 4) % 5 replaces (i - 1) % 5 so C's negative modulo doesn't index state[-1]!

1. The Readers-Writers Problem (Silberschatz §7.1.2)

A shared database or file is accessed concurrently by Readers (who only inspect data) and Writers (who both read and modify data):

  • Multiple Readers may read simultaneously without harming consistency.
  • A Writer requires strict exclusive access: no other Reader and no other Writer may be active while a Writer updates.

First Readers-Writers (Reader Priority)

No Reader is kept waiting unless a Writer already holds the database.

semaphore rw_mutex = 1; // locks DB for writers
semaphore mutex = 1;    // guards read_count
int read_count = 0;

// WRITER PROCESS:
while (true) {
    wait(rw_mutex);
    /* writing is performed */
    signal(rw_mutex);
}

Reader Process (First R-W Solution)

while (true) {
    wait(mutex);
    read_count++;
    if (read_count == 1)
        wait(rw_mutex); // 1st reader locks out writers
    signal(mutex);

    /* reading is performed (N concurrent readers!) */

    wait(mutex);
    read_count--;
    if (read_count == 0)
        signal(rw_mutex); // last reader unlocks writers
    signal(mutex);
}
⚠️ Starvation Analysis: First vs. Second Readers-Writers & Kernel RW-Locks
  • First Readers-Writers Weakness: While Reader 1 is still reading, Readers 2, 3, 4… keep entering so read_count never drops back to 0! Waiting Writers may starve indefinitely!
  • Second Readers-Writers Variant: Once a Writer is ready, no new Readers may start reading; waiting Writers jump ahead. Trade-off: Now Readers may starve behind a steady stream of Writers!
  • Modern OS Solution (Reader-Writer Locks): Systems like Linux/POSIX (pthread_rwlock_t) provide dedicated reader-writer locks useful whenever reading dominates writing (>80% reads) and typically enforce FIFO queueing to avoid starving either side.

2. The Dining Philosophers Problem (Silberschatz §7.1.3)

Five philosophers sit around a circular table with 5 single chopsticks (semaphore chopstick[5] = {1,1,1,1,1};) placed between each pair. To eat, philosopher i needs both left chopstick i and right chopstick (i + 1) % 5.

// NAIVE BROKEN SOLUTION FOR PHILOSOPHER i:
while (true) {
    wait(chopstick[i]);            // grab left chopstick
    wait(chopstick[(i + 1) % 5]);  // grab right chopstick
    /* eat for awhile */
    signal(chopstick[i]);          // put down left
    signal(chopstick[(i + 1) % 5]);// put down right
    /* think for awhile */
}

Why It Deadlocks: If all 5 philosophers grow hungry simultaneously and execute wait(chopstick[i]) before any reaches the second wait, all 5 elements of chopstick[] become 0. Now all 5 philosophers block forever on chopstick[(i+1)%5] holding 1 chopstick each—forming a textbook Circular Wait Deadlock!

3. All Four Deadlock Remedies (§7.1.3.1 Semaphore Remedies & §7.1.3.2 Monitor)

Remedy (§7.1.3)MechanismDeadlock-Free?Starvation-Free?
1. Seat Cap (≤ 4)Allow at most 4 philosophers at a 5-chopstick table via counting semaphore room = 4. (Pigeonhole principle: at least 1 gets both!)YESNot guaranteed
2. All-or-Nothing Critical SectionPhilosopher picks up chopsticks only if both are free inside a mutex lock.YESNO (conspiracy / starvation possible)
3. Asymmetric Pickup OrderOdd-numbered philosophers pick up Left first then Right; Even-numbered pick up Right first then Left! (Breaks circular symmetry!)YESNot guaranteed
4. Monitor State Solution (§7.1.3.2, textbook)Philosophers enter a Monitor only picking up chopsticks if neither neighbor is EATING.YESNO (Silberschatz §7.1.3.2: alternating neighbors can still starve a philosopher!)
 
monitor DiningPhilosophers {
    enum { THINKING, HUNGRY, EATING } state[5];
    condition self[5];

    void test(int i) {
        if ((state[(i + 4) % 5] != EATING) &&
            (state[i] == HUNGRY) &&
            (state[(i + 1) % 5] != EATING)) {
            state[i] = EATING;
            self[i].signal(); // wakes Pi if hungry, no effect during putdown if neighbor already awake
        }
    }
    void pickup(int i) {
        state[i] = HUNGRY;
        test(i);
        if (state[i] != EATING) self[i].wait();
    }
    void putdown(int i) {
        state[i] = THINKING;
        test((i + 4) % 5); // test LEFT neighbor
        test((i + 1) % 5); // test RIGHT neighbor
    }
    initialization_code() { for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) state[i] = THINKING; }
}

Exam Proof Insight (§7.1.3.2): No two adjacent neighbors can ever eat simultaneously because test(i) enforces state[(i+4)%5] != EATING and state[(i+1)%5] != EATING! Even better, putdown(i) directly tests both neighbors—guaranteeing deadlock freedom cleanly. However, Silberschatz §7.1.3.2 explicitly cautions that starvation is still possible here (e.g., if P0 and P2 alternate holding EATING state while P1 stays HUNGRY); note also Slide 12 stops after the 3 Semaphore remedies (§7.1.3.1).

deck_13.html:
DECK 13 · DEADLOCK FOUNDATIONS · SILBERSCHATZ CH. 8 (§8.1–§8.5)

Deadlock Characterization, Resource-Allocation Graphs (RAG) & Prevention

Silberschatz 10th Ed. Chapter 8 (§8.1–§8.5) · CPCS-361 Final Exam Core
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Define Deadlock rigorously and distinguish Deadlock (blocked Waiting state) from Livelock (running, repeatedly retrying and failing) (§8.1–§8.2.1).
  • State all 4 Coffman Necessary Conditions that must hold simultaneously for deadlock (§8.3.1).
  • Construct and analyze Resource-Allocation Graphs (RAG) with Request Edges and Assignment Edges (§8.3.2).
  • Distinguish between Single-Instance RAG (cycle = deadlock) vs. Multi-Instance RAG (cycle ≠ always deadlock!).
  • Compare OS handling strategies (§8.4) and design Deadlock Prevention protocols breaking each of the 4 Coffman conditions, especially Total Resource Ordering (§8.5.4).
💡 Intuition First: Kansas Trains, Hallway Dance & Two-Lane Roundabouts
  • Naive Fixes → Visible Failure: Replacing blocking locks with non-blocking pthread_mutex_trylock() + release-and-retry (§8.2.1 Fig. 8.2) cures deadlock yet falls into Livelock whenever threads retry in lockstep! Trying to break Mutual Exclusion or Hold-and-Wait naively either corrupts non-shareable writes or starves resource utilization. Even static parameter ordering transfer(from, to) still deadlocks on concurrent opposing calls unless ordered by immutable unique object ID (§8.5.4 Fig. 8.7)!
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: Deadlock is the old Kansas railway joke: two trains halted forever at a crossing because neither may move until the other has passed; Livelock is two overly polite people stepping left-right identically in a hallway without moving forward; a Multi-Instance RAG cycle without deadlock (Fig. 8.6) is a 2-lane traffic circle—even if two inner-lane cars wait on each other, an outer-lane car (T2 or T4) exits freely and opens a lane! Where street-sign analogies break: Static lock numbering fails when arguments swap roles dynamically (Acct_A → Acct_B vs Acct_B → Acct_A)—order must compare immutable IDs (min(id) → max(id)).
  • Why Each Rule Exists: Total Ordering F: R → N makes a closed loop impossible because ascending order along a cycle forces F(R0) < F(R1) < … < F(R0) (contradiction!). Cycle = guaranteed deadlock only with 1 instance per box because zero spare outer lanes exist!

1. System Model & Deadlock vs. Livelock (§8.1–§8.2.1)

A system contains resource types R1, R2, …, Rm (CPU cycles, memory space, files, mutex locks), each having Wi indistinguishable instances (Slide 13 notes shareable resources like read-only files never cause deadlocks, while non-shareable ones like printers or mutexes do). Every thread utilizes a resource in 3 strict phases: Request → Use → Release.

Deadlock occurs when every thread in a set is permanently blocked (Waiting state) waiting for an event that only another thread inside the exact same blocked set can cause (§8.2 discusses multithreaded mutex deadlocks). Contrast with Livelock (§8.2.1) (two people politely stepping left-right in sync in a hallway forever): threads are actively executing and repeatedly failing/retrying rather than sleeping, solvable via randomized exponential backoff.

2. The Four Necessary Coffman Conditions (§8.3.1)

📜 Textbook Theorem: Necessary Conditions for Deadlock
All four conditions must hold simultaneously in a system for a deadlock to arise. Breaking any single one guarantees deadlock cannot occur:
  1. Mutual Exclusion: At least one resource must be held in a non-sharable mode (only one thread can use an instance at any instant; e.g., mutex lock or printer).
  2. Hold and Wait: A thread must currently be holding at least one resource while waiting to acquire additional resources currently held by other threads.
  3. No Preemption: Resources cannot be forcibly taken away; a resource can only be released voluntarily by the thread holding it after completing its task.
  4. Circular Wait: A closed chain of waiting threads {T0, T1, …, Tn} exists such that T0 waits for a resource held by T1, T1 waits for T2, …, and Tn waits for a resource held by T0. (Note: Circular Wait implies Hold and Wait!)

3. Resource-Allocation Graphs (RAG — §8.3.2)

A directed bipartite graph G = (V, E) where vertices partition into Threads/Processes T = {T1, …, Tn} (circles; Slide 13 writes P1..Pn) and Resource Types R = {R1, …, Rm} (rectangles containing dots for instances):

  • Request Edge (Ti → Rj): Directed from thread to resource box edge; thread Ti has requested an instance of Rj and is waiting.
  • Assignment Edge (Rj → Ti): Directed from a specific instance dot inside Rj to thread Ti; an instance of Rj has been allocated to Ti.
EXAMPLE A — MULTI-INSTANCE WITH DEADLOCK (Fig. 8.4–8.5): EXAMPLE B — MULTI-INSTANCE CYCLE, NO DEADLOCK (Fig. 8.6): R1 (1 dot → T2), R3 (1 dot → T3) T1 ──req──> R1 (2 dots: Dot1 → T2, Dot2 → T3) R2 (2 dots: Dot1 → T1, Dot2 → T2), R4 (3 free dots) T3 ──req──> R2 (2 dots: Dot1 → T1, Dot2 → T4) Requests: T1 → R1, T2 → R3, T3 → R2 (triggers jam!) [Cycle: T1 → R1 → T3 → R2 → T1 exists!] Cycles: T1→R1→T2→R3→T3→R2→T1 AND T2→R3→T3→R2→T2 ⇒ NOT DEADLOCKED! Why? T2 & T4 hold NO requests! ⇒ T1, T2, T3 form locked cycles (NO free escape!). T4 finishes & frees R2 → T3 runs → frees R1 → T1 runs!
Graph ObservationSingle-Instance ResourcesMulti-Instance Resources
No Cycle in RAGNO DEADLOCKNO DEADLOCK
Cycle Exists in RAGDEFINITE DEADLOCK (Cycle is necessary & sufficient!)MAY OR MAY NOT BE DEADLOCKED (Cycle is necessary, NOT sufficient!)

4. Approaches & Deadlock Prevention (§8.4–§8.5)

OS designers handle deadlocks via (§8.4): (1) Prevention / Avoidance (ensure system never enters deadlock), (2) Detection & Recovery (detect and break deadlocks), or (3) Ignore ("Ostrich Algorithm"—Linux, Windows, UNIX treat rare programmer deadlocks as application bugs).

Deadlock Prevention (§8.5) constrains how requests are made so at least one Coffman condition cannot possibly hold:

Coffman Condition TargetedPrevention Mechanism (§8.5.1–§8.5.4)Practical Feasibility / Drawback
1. Break Mutual ExclusionMake resources inherently sharable (e.g., read-only files).Often Impossible! Mutexes and write-locks are intrinsically non-sharable.
2. Break Hold & WaitProtocol A: Request & acquire all resources before starting.
Protocol B: Allow requesting new resources only when holding none (release all held first).		Low resource utilization (locks idle for hours) + risk of Starvation if popular resource sets are contested.
3. Break No PreemptionIf Ti holds R1 and requests busy R2 that cannot be granted immediately, implicitly release all resources Ti currently holds (or preempt R2 from another waiting thread).Only works cleanly when state is easy to save/restore (CPU registers, memory pages); breaks down for mutexes/printers.
4. Break Circular WaitTotal Ordering F: R → N: Assign every resource type a unique integer ID (e.g., F(mutex1)=1, F(mutex2)=5) and require threads to acquire resources strictly in increasing numerical order!MOST PRACTICAL IN REAL KERNELS! Proof: Suppose a cycle existed: F(R0) < F(R1) < … < F(Rn) < F(R0) ⇒ F(R0) < F(R0), impossible contradiction! (Gotcha: Hierarchical locks like lock(A); lock(B) don't cover dynamic parameters like transfer(from, to) unless ordered by min(id) → max(id)).

deck_14.html:
DECK 14 · DYNAMIC RESOURCE SAFETY · SILBERSCHATZ §8.6

Deadlock Avoidance, Safe States & The Banker's Algorithm (Full Matrix Trace)

Silberschatz 10th Ed. Chapter 8 (§8.6) · CPCS-361 Final Exam Core Numerical Problem
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Compare Deadlock Prevention (static rules) vs. Deadlock Avoidance (dynamic a priori max-claim examination) (§8.6).
  • Define Safe State, Unsafe State, and Deadlock State rigorously (and know why Unsafe ≠ Deadlock!) (§8.6.1, Fig. 8.8).
  • Use Claim Edges in single-instance Resource-Allocation Graphs (Fig. 8.9–8.10, §8.6.2).
  • Compute the Need Matrix and execute both phases of Dijkstra's Banker's Algorithm (Safety + Resource-Request) (§8.6.3).
💡 Intuition First: The Small-Town Banker & The 12-Tape Cliff
  • Naive Greedy Allocation → Visible Failure (§8.6.1): Suppose 12 resources exist, T0/T1/T2 declare Max (10, 4, 9) and hold (5, 2, 2), leaving Available = 3 (<T1, T0, T2> is Safe). Now T2 requests 1 unit—plenty sit free (3 ≥ 1)! Yet granting greedily leaves Available = 2: after T1 finishes, free supply is only 4, which satisfies neither T0 (needs up to 5 more) nor T2 (needs up to 6 more) → potential deadlock!
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: Dijkstra modeled a cautious small-town banker (§8.6.3): each customer pre-registers a maximum credit limit (Max), already borrowed Allocation, and can still draw Need = Max − Allocation. Even if cash sits in the vault today, the banker simulates granting the loan to check whether at least ONE sequential repayment ladder exists where every customer finishes and repays in full! Where the analogy breaks: Unlike contracted bank credit lines, real OS processes rarely know their exact lifetime Max upfront, AND an Unsafe State is not yet bankrupt (Fig. 8.8)—processes might release early without drawing their full Max!
  • Why Each Rule Exists: Work = Work + Allocation[i] simulates Ti completing its worst-case Need[i] and returning every unit it holds to the vault; rolling back an UNSAFE pretend grant proves why "available right now ≠ safe tomorrow."

1. Safe State vs. Unsafe State vs. Deadlock (§8.6.1)

Instead of rigid global restrictions, Deadlock Avoidance asks every process to declare a priori the maximum number of instances of each resource type it may ever need. Before granting any request, the OS checks whether granting keeps the system in a Safe State.

📜 Textbook Definition: Safe State & Safe Sequence
A state is safe if the system can allocate resources to each thread (up to its declared maximum) in some order and still avoid deadlock—specifically, there exists a Safe Sequence <T0, T1, …, Tn−1> where for every Ti, the resources Ti can still request can be satisfied by currently available resources plus all resources held by earlier threads Tj (j < i).
STATE SPACE DIAGRAM (Silberschatz Fig. 8.8): ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ UNSAFE STATES │ │ ┌──────────────┐ │ │ │ DEADLOCK │ ← Unsafe means "can reach deadlock │ │ └──────────────┘ IF processes request their Max!" │ ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ SAFE STATES │ │ (GUARANTEED zero deadlocks!) │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Exam Traps: (1) A Safe state is never deadlocked. (2) An Unsafe state is NOT automatically a deadlock! Processes might exit early without requesting their remaining Max; however, the OS cannot prevent deadlock if processes suddenly demand their full declared Max. (3) Multiple safe sequences can exist for the same system snapshot.

2. Single-Instance Avoidance: Claim Edges (§8.6.2, Fig. 8.9–8.10)

For single-instance resources, add dashed Claim Edges (Ti → Rj) showing that Ti may request Rj in the future. When Ti requests Rj, the dashed Claim Edge converts to a solid Request Edge; when Rj is granted, it converts to an Assignment Edge. Avoidance Rule: Grant the request only if converting the Request Edge to an Assignment Edge creates no cycle in the RAG (cycle detection runs in O(n2)). Textbook Worked Trace (Fig. 8.9–8.10 / Slide 14): Suppose T1 holds R1 and claims R2, while T2 requests R1 and claims R2. If R2 is still free and T2 asks for R2, converting it yields cycle R1 → T1 → R2 → T2 → R1 → UNSAFE & DENIED; if T1 asks for R2 first, zero cycle forms → SAFE & GRANTED!

3. The Banker's Algorithm Data Structures (§8.6.3)

For multiple-instance resource systems (n threads, m resource types), Dijkstra named this after a cautious small-town banker who never allocates cash so he can no longer satisfy all customers' credit lines:

  • Available[m]: Vector of currently free instances of each resource type.
  • Max[n][m]: Maximum demand declared upfront by each thread.
  • Allocation[n][m]: Instances currently held by each thread.
  • Need[n][m]: Remaining potential future need of each thread:
Need[i][j] = Max[i][j] − Allocation[i][j]

Algorithm 1: Safety Algorithm — O(m × n2)

1. Work[0..m-1] = Available;
   Finish[0..n-1] = false;
2. Find index i such that:
   Finish[i] == false  AND  Need[i] <= Work
   (if no such i exists, go to Step 4)
3. Work = Work + Allocation[i];
   Finish[i] = true;
   Append Ti to SafeSequence; go to Step 2
4. If Finish[i] == true for ALL i ⇒ SAFE STATE!
   Otherwise ⇒ UNSAFE STATE!

Algorithm 2: Resource-Request for Ti

1. If Request[i] > Need[i]:
     raise ERROR (exceeded max claim!)
2. If Request[i] > Available:
     T_i must WAIT (not enough free now)
3. Pretend to allocate (tentative snapshot):
     Available   = Available   - Request[i]
     Allocation[i] = Allocation[i] + Request[i]
     Need[i]     = Need[i]     - Request[i]
4. Run Safety Algorithm on tentative state:
     • If SAFE   ⇒ COMMIT & GRANT request!
     • If UNSAFE ⇒ ROLL BACK & block T_i!

4. Complete Textbook Worked Example (Silberschatz §8.6.3.3 & Slide 14)

System has 5 threads/processes (Silberschatz 10th Ed. names them T0..T4; Slide 14 names them P0..P4) and 3 resource types: A = 10, B = 5, C = 7 instances. Initial Snapshot at T0:

ThreadAllocation (A B C)Max (A B C)Available (A B C)Computed Need = Max − Alloc
P00  1  07  5  33  3  2
(Total − ΣAlloc:
10−7=3, 5−2=3, 7−5=2)		7  4  3
P12  0  03  2  21  2  2
P23  0  29  0  26  0  0
P32  1  12  2  20  1  1
P40  0  24  3  34  3  1
🧮 Part A: Proving Initial Snapshot is SAFE (Safety Trace)

Start with Work = (3, 3, 2), Finish = [F, F, F, F, F]:

  1. Need[P0] = (7,4,3) ≤ (3,3,2)? No. Check P1: Need[P1] = (1,2,2) ≤ (3,3,2) ⇒ YES! Run P1; reclaim Allocation(2,0,0): Work = (3,3,2) + (2,0,0) = (5, 3, 2).
  2. Check P3: Need[P3] = (0,1,1) ≤ (5,3,2) ⇒ YES! Reclaim (2,1,1): Work = (5,3,2) + (2,1,1) = (7, 4, 3).
  3. Check P4: Need[P4] = (4,3,1) ≤ (7,4,3) ⇒ YES! Reclaim (0,0,2): Work = (7,4,3) + (0,0,2) = (7, 4, 5).
  4. Check P2: Need[P2] = (6,0,0) ≤ (7,4,5) ⇒ YES! Reclaim (3,0,2): Work = (7,4,5) + (3,0,2) = (10, 4, 7).
  5. Check P0: Need[P0] = (7,4,3) ≤ (10,4,7) ⇒ YES! Reclaim (0,1,0): Work = (10, 5, 7) (= Total Resources!).
Conclusion: All Finish[i] == true! Valid Safe Sequence: <P1, P3, P4, P2, P0> ⇒ System is SAFE! (Exam Note: Silberschatz §8.6.3.3 writes <T1, T3, T4, T2, T0> and Slide 14 chooses <P1, P3, P4, P0, P2>—any valid full permutation proves the state Safe!)
🧮 Part B: Evaluating New Requests from T0
  • Case 1 — P1 requests (1, 0, 2):
    Check (1,0,2) ≤ Need[P1]=(1,2,2) (OK) & (1,0,2) ≤ Available=(3,3,2) (OK).
    Pretend state: Available = (2, 3, 0), Alloc[P1] = (3, 0, 2), Need[P1] = (0, 2, 0).
    Run Safety: P1 (Need 0,2,0 ≤ 2,3,0 → Work 5,3,2) → P3 (Work 7,4,3) → P4 (Work 7,4,5) → P0 (Work 7,5,5) → P2 (Work 10,5,7). Sequence <P1, P3, P4, P0, P2> exists ⇒ REQUEST GRANTED!
  • Case 2 — Starting from Case 1 state, P4 requests (3, 3, 0):
    Check (3,3,0) ≤ Available=(2,3,0)? FALSE (3 > 2 for Resource A)! Rejected immediately (P4 must wait—not enough free A).
  • Case 3 — Starting from Case 1 state, P0 requests (0, 2, 0):
    Check (0,2,0) ≤ Available=(2,3,0) (OK). Pretend Available = (2, 1, 0). Run Safety: every process's Need exceeds (2,1,0) (e.g., Need[P1]=(0,2,0) needs B=2, only B=1 left; Need[P3]=(0,1,1) needs C=1, only C=0 left!). Zero threads can finish ⇒ UNSAFE STATE ⇒ DENIED & ROLLED BACK!

deck_15.html:
DECK 15 · DETECTION & RECOVERY · SILBERSCHATZ §8.7–§8.8

Deadlock Detection Algorithms & System Recovery Strategies

Silberschatz 10th Ed. Chapter 8 (§8.7–§8.8) · CPCS-361 Final Exam Core
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Contrast Deadlock Avoidance (needs future Max) with Deadlock Detection (evaluates current Request only) (§8.7).
  • Construct a Wait-For Graph (WFG) from a single-instance RAG and detect cycles in O(n2) (§8.7.1, Fig. 8.11).
  • Execute the Multi-Instance Detection Algorithm using Available, Allocation, and Request matrices and identify exact deadlocked processes (§8.7.2).
  • Select detection frequency wisely based on deadlock frequency and rollback cost (§8.7.3).
  • Compare Process Termination vs. Resource Preemption recovery (Rollback + Starvation prevention) (§8.8).
💡 Intuition First: Traffic Audits Without Destination Maps & Why Cost Must Escalate
  • Naive Fixes → Visible Failure: Collapsing resources into a Wait-For Graph (Ti → Tj) works for 1-instance resources yet fails on multi-instance pools because it hides spare free instances! Conversely, Banker's Safety fails because processes never declared Max! And after detecting a jam, always preempting the statically "cheapest" victim creates Recovery Starvation (§8.8.2) because the same tiny process keeps getting aborted forever!
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: Multi-Instance Detection is an intersection traffic audit without trip manifests: inspectors only look at which single lane each car is asking for right now (Request). Any car parked empty-handed (Allocation == 0) or whose next meter has room (Request ≤ Work) is optimistically assumed to drive away and free its spots; everyone still stranded when scanning stops forms the deadlocked pileup. Where the analogy breaks: Unlike Banker's Avoidance (which stays safe all the way to exit), Detection's pass verdict is purely optimistic (§8.7.2)—a car with Request == 0 right now might request a locked resource milliseconds later!
  • Why Each Formula Exists: Finish[i] = (Allocation[i] == 0) starts idle-handed threads finished because they hold zero instances anyone else could wait on; adding rollback_count into victim cost guarantees every rollback raises that thread's preemption price until it stops being targeted (§8.8.2).

1. Single-Instance Detection: The Wait-For Graph (§8.7.1, Fig. 8.11)

If an OS applies neither prevention nor avoidance, it must periodically detect deadlocks and recover. When every resource type has only one instance, simplify the RAG by collapsing all resource vertices: draw directed edge Ti → Tj if and only if thread Ti is waiting for a resource currently assigned to thread Tj.

SIMPLE CHAIN: T1 → R1 → T2 → R2 → T3 → R3 → T1 ⇒ WFG: T1 → T2 → T3 → T1 (Cycle = DEADLOCK!) SILBERSCHATZ FIG. 8.11 / SLIDE 15 (5-Process WFG): P1 → P2, P2 → {P3, P4, P5}, P3 → P4, P4 → P1 ⇒ Cycles: P1→P2→P4→P1 and P1→P2→P3→P4→P1!

A deadlock exists in the single-instance system if and only if the Wait-For Graph contains a cycle. Cycle detection takes O(n2) operations (where n is the number of threads).

2. Multi-Instance Detection Algorithm (§8.7.2)

When resources have multiple instances, Wait-For Graphs are insufficient. Instead, we use a matrix test similar to Banker's Safety Algorithm—with two crucial differences:

  1. We use Request[i][j] (current outstanding request, not future Need/Max, since avoidance isn't used!).
  2. Optimistic Initialization: Threads currently holding zero resources (Allocationi == 0) cannot be holding anything anyone waits on, so Finish[i] = true initially; otherwise Finish[i] = false!
1. Work = Available;
   for i = 0..n-1: Finish[i] = (Allocation[i] == 0) ? true : false;
2. Find index i such that:
     Finish[i] == false  AND  Request[i] <= Work
   (if no such i exists, go to Step 4)
3. Optimistic assumption: T_i finishes without further waits!
     Work = Work + Allocation[i];
     Finish[i] = true;  go to Step 2
4. If Finish[i] == false for ANY i:
     System IS DEADLOCKED, and EVERY thread with Finish[i] == false IS IN THE DEADLOCK!
🧮 Complete Worked Multi-Instance Detection Example (Silberschatz §8.7.2)

Given 5 threads P0..P4, 3 resource types (A=7, B=2, C=6), and Available = (0, 0, 0):

ThreadAllocation (A B C)Request (A B C)Trace Step
P00 1 00 0 0Request[P0]=(0,0,0) ≤ Work(0,0,0) → Runs! New Work = (0,1,0)
P12 0 02 0 2Request[P1]=(2,0,2) > Work(0,0,0) → Waits on pass 1 (runs last once Work=(5,2,6)!)
P23 0 30 0 0Request[P2]=(0,0,0) ≤ Work(0,1,0) → Runs! New Work = (3,1,3)
P32 1 11 0 0Request[P3]=(1,0,0) ≤ Work(3,1,3) → Runs! New Work = (5,2,4)
P40 0 20 0 2Request[P4]=(0,0,2) ≤ Work(5,2,4) → Runs! New Work = (5,2,6)

Now only P1 remains (Request=(2,0,2) ≤ Work(5,2,6)) → Runs too! No deadlock! Completion order <P0, P2, P3, P4, P1> (Silberschatz §8.7.2 traces <T0, T2, T3, T1, T4>; note Slide 15 loosely calls this a "Safe Sequence" though Detection has no Max claims!).
Now suppose P2 makes ONE extra request for C: Request[P2] = (0, 0, 1): Starting with Work=(0,0,0), only P0 can run (Work=(0,1,0)). Now NO remaining thread's Request fits (0,1,0)! Detection stops with Finish = [T, F, F, F, F] ⇒ DEADLOCK involving {P1, P2, P3, P4}!

3. When to Invoke Detection? (§8.7.3)

Running an O(m × n2) check on every failed request causes overhead (only at the extreme "every request that cannot be granted immediately" can you spot both the deadlocked set and the single culprit!). Two practical alternatives (§8.7.3): (1) Run periodically (e.g., once per hour), or (2) Trigger only when CPU utilization drops below a threshold (say 40%). Note: running detection only periodically means a cycle may pull in innocent later threads before being caught, making it harder to identify which thread originally caused the jam.

4. Deadlock Recovery Strategies (§8.8)

Option A: Process Termination (§8.8.1)

1. Abort ALL deadlocked processes: Fast & guaranteed to break cycle, but extremely expensive (discards partial hours of work).
2. Abort ONE process at a time and re-run detection until cycle breaks: lower wasted work, higher detection overhead. Choose victim with lowest cost based on (5 textbook factors + Slide 15 #6):

  • Priority of the process
  • How long it has run & how much longer to finish
  • Types & count of resources held (and whether preemptible)
  • How many more resources it still needs to finish
  • How many processes would need to be terminated
  • Slide 15 (#6): Interactive vs. batch process

Option B: Resource Preemption (§8.8.2)

Successively confiscate resources from victim processes and give them to others until deadlock breaks. Requires addressing 3 critical issues:

  1. Selecting a Victim: Minimize cost (held resource count, execution time consumed so far).
  2. Rollback: Process cannot continue cleanly missing a stolen lock/file! Must perform either Total Rollback (abort & restart from scratch) or Partial Rollback (restore to last saved checkpoint—requires kernel/DB checkpointing!).
  3. Preventing Starvation: If the same process keeps getting picked as cheapest victim, it never finishes! Fix: Include the count of rollbacks in the cost metric so repeated victims grow prohibitively expensive to kill!

deck_16.html:
DECK 16 · CONTIGUOUS MEMORY ARCHITECTURE · SILBERSCHATZ CH. 9 (§9.1–§9.2, §9.5)

Address Binding, Hardware Protection, Dynamic Allocation, Fragmentation & Swapping

Silberschatz 10th Ed. Chapter 9 (§9.1–§9.2, §9.5) · CPCS-361 Final Exam Core
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Enforce OS-level memory protection cleanly using hardware Base and Limit Registers (§9.1.1).
  • Compare all 3 Address Binding stages: Compile Time, Load Time, and Execution Time (§9.1.2).
  • Differentiate Logical (Virtual) vs. Physical Addresses translated dynamically by the MMU (§9.1.3).
  • Explain Dynamic Loading vs. Dynamic Linking (Shared Libraries / DLLs) (§9.1.4–§9.1.5).
  • Trace First-Fit, Best-Fit, and Worst-Fit hole allocation (Slide 16 variable/fixed traces & §9.2.2) and distinguish Internal vs. External Fragmentation, Compaction (§9.2.3), and Swapping (§9.5).
💡 Intuition First: Parallel-Parked Cars Along One Curb
  • Naive Attempts → Visible Failure: Letting programs compile fixed physical addresses (§9.1.3) crashes whenever two apps load at 0x1000, and sharing RAM without hardware bounds lets one bad pointer overwrite the kernel. Even with relocation + bounds, dynamic variable partitions carve free RAM into scattered small holes (§9.2.3)—on Slide 16's 2400-unit memory trace, P4 = 350 fails under First-Fit despite 360 free units!
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: Contiguous variable allocation is parallel parking cars of unequal length along one 2,400-foot curb: your Base (Relocation) Register marks your rear bumper's zero-point; your Limit Register enforces your car's legal bay length; Compaction asks every parked car to pull forward simultaneously to squeeze empty curb gaps together. Where the analogy breaks: Running CPU threads and DMA hardware hold live addresses, so Compaction requires execution-time dynamic binding plus routing pending I/O strictly through OS kernel buffers (Slide 16 double-buffering note), while Swapping (§9.5) hauls idle cars onto a slow off-street disk lot (4,000 ms for 100 MB @ 50 MB/s)!
  • Why Each Rule Exists: Why Swapping pays 2 × (Size / Rate) (evict victim + reload entrant); why Best-Fit usually increases tiny dust fragments even though Slide 16's exact trace lets P4=350 squeeze through cleanly.

1. Base & Limit Registers and Hardware Protection (§9.1.1)

Before running any user process, the OS must guarantee no user process overwrites kernel memory or another process's RAM. Hardware enforces this via two dedicated registers checked on every single CPU memory fetch/store in User Mode:

  • Base Register: Holds the smallest legal physical memory address assigned to the process.
  • Limit Register: Specifies the size of the legal contiguous range. Valid physical addresses satisfy: Base ≤ Address < Base + Limit.
  • Only the OS running in Kernel Mode (Mode Bit = 0) can load Base/Limit registers via privileged instructions. Any out-of-bounds user access triggers an immediate addressing error trap to the OS!

2. Address Binding Stages & Logical vs. Physical Addresses (§9.1.2–§9.1.3)

Binding StageWhen Physical Address Is DecidedConsequence / Flexibility
1. Compile TimeAbsolute physical address known at compile time.Generates absolute code (e.g., old MS-DOS .com). If start address shifts later, program must be recompiled!
2. Load TimePhysical location unknown at compile time; compiler emits relocatable code.Loader fixes addresses once when loading into RAM. Cannot move process in RAM once running!
3. Execution TimeProcess can move between physical segments while executing!Used by ALL modern OSes! Requires Memory Management Unit (MMU) hardware mapping.

Logical vs. Physical Address: The address generated by the CPU is a Logical Address (0 to max); the address placed onto the memory bus for RAM chips is a Physical Address. Under Compile-Time and Load-Time binding, logical == physical. Under Execution-Time binding, they differ (logical is called a virtual address), and the hardware MMU adds the Relocation Register (= Base) at runtime: Physical = Logical + Relocation_Register. User programs deal exclusively with logical addresses and never see real physical addresses!

Dynamic Loading vs. Dynamic Linking: Dynamic Loading delays loading infrequently called routines (e.g., error handlers) from disk until actually invoked—reducing memory footprint without OS kernel help. Dynamic Linking & Shared Libraries (.so on Linux, .dll on Windows) postpones linking external library code until execution via a tiny memory stub, allowing multiple running processes to share one physical RAM copy of standard library code (requires OS assistance for shared read-only pages).

3. Contiguous Memory Allocation & Fit Strategies (§9.2)

Main memory typically holds the OS (low memory with Interrupt Vector) and multiple user processes in high memory. In Variable-Partition (Dynamic) Contiguous Allocation, the OS tracks allocated blocks and a linked list of free holes. When a new process of size S arrives, three classic heuristics pick which hole (≥ S) to allocate:

StrategySelection RuleStrength vs. Weakness
First-FitAllocate the first hole scanned from the start that is big enough.Fastest scan; good overall utilization, tends to leave small fragments near front.
Best-FitAllocate the smallest hole that is still big enough (searches full list unless sorted).Saves huge holes, BUT creates tiny unusable leftover slivers (worst external fragmentation!).
Worst-FitAllocate the largest available hole (searches full list unless sorted).Leftover pieces stay large enough to reuse, yet breaks up huge contiguous blocks quickly.
🧮 Worked Allocation Traces (Slide 16 Variable Trace & Practice Exercise)

1. Slide 16 Variable-Partition Trace (Total RAM = 2,400 units after initial OS/jobs; requests P8=115, P9=500, P6=35, P1=200, P4=350):
• First-Fit: Int Frag = 0, Ext Frag = 360 (holes 210 + 150) → P4 (350) FAILS!
• Best-Fit: Int Frag = 0, Ext Frag = 10 → P4 (350) SUCCEEDS! (Also check Slide 16 Fixed Same-Size 20 MB partitions with P1=8, P2=17, P3=20 MB ⇒ 12+3+0 = 15 MB internal fragmentation, and Varying Fixed Partitions matching 10th Ed. Practice Ex. 9.6 holes 300, 600, 350, 200, 750, 125 KB).
• Worst-Fit: Int Frag = 0, Ext Frag = 360 (150 + 115 + 95) → P4 (350) FAILS!

2. Classic Edition Hole Problem (Holes = 100K, 500K, 200K, 300K, 600K; Requests P1=212K, P2=417K, P3=112K, P4=426K):

  • First-Fit: P1→500K (288K left), P2→600K (183K left), P3→288K (176K left), P4 (426K) → MUST WAIT!
  • Best-Fit: P1→300K (88K), P2→500K (83K), P3→200K (88K), P4→600K (174K)! ALL 4 SUCCEED!
  • Worst-Fit: P1→600K (388K), P2→500K (83K), P3→388K (276K), P4 (426K) → MUST WAIT!

4. Internal vs. External Fragmentation, Compaction & Swapping (§9.2.3 & §9.5)

External Fragmentation (§9.2.3)

Enough total free memory exists across RAM to satisfy a request, but it is scattered into non-contiguous small holes too small individually.
50-Percent Rule (First-Fit): Statistically, given N allocated blocks, another 0.5N blocks are lost to fragmentation—i.e., 1/3 of all RAM is unusable!
Remedies: (1) Compaction (shuffle allocated blocks together—ONLY works with execution-time dynamic binding, expensive I/O copy!), or (2) Non-Contiguous Paging.

Internal Fragmentation & Swapping (§9.5)

Internal Fragmentation (§9.2.3): Unused wasted bytes inside an already allocated fixed-size block/partition (e.g., allocating a 18,464-byte block when a process only needed 18,462 bytes wastes 2 bytes because tracking micro-holes costs more overhead than leaving them attached).
Swapping (§9.5): Temporarily rolling idle processes (or pages) out of RAM to a fast backing store on disk and bringing them back later—Slide 16 timing trace: swapping a 100 MB process over a 50 MB/s bus takes 2000 ms out + 2000 ms in = 4,000 ms (4 s), and pending I/O must target OS kernel buffers!

deck_17.html:
DECK 17 · NON-CONTIGUOUS MEMORY · SILBERSCHATZ CH. 9 (§9.3–§9.4)

Paging Architecture, TLB Hardware, Effective Access Time, Page Tables & Segmentation

Silberschatz 10th Ed. Chapter 9 (§9.3–§9.4) & Lecture Slide 17 · CPCS-361 Final Exam Core Calculations
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Explain why Paging eliminates External Fragmentation completely (while retaining Internal Fragmentation only on the final page, e.g., 962 B on Slide 17) (§9.3.1).
  • Translate logical addresses (p, d) into physical addresses (f, d) using binary bit-splitting and decimal division (incl. Slide 17 Sample Q1 & Q2) (§9.3.1).
  • Calculate Effective Access Time (EAT) using the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) hit ratio α (§9.3.2).
  • Interpret Valid-Invalid bits, protection bits (Read/Write/Execute), Shared Pages, and ASIDs (§9.3.3–§9.3.4).
  • Compare Hierarchical (Multi-Level), Hashed, and Inverted Page Tables (§9.4), plus hardware Segmentation (STBR/STLR, Slide 17).
💡 Intuition First: Loose-Leaf Bindings & Sticky-Note Speed Dials
  • Naive Solutions → Visible Failure: Storing a process as uniform fixed pages inside non-contiguous frames cures external fragmentation completely—yet storing a flat Page Table in RAM forces two RAM trips per byte (50% slowdown!). Worse, on 64-bit systems a flat page table demands 252 entries per process—impossible to allocate contiguously!
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: Think of Paging as slicing a bound book (logical address space) into uniform loose-leaf sheets housed in random library shelves (frames), tracked by an index binder (page table) plus a tiny desk-side sticky-note speed dial (TLB, 32–1,024 hot shortcuts). Where the analogy breaks: Unlike human eyes scanning a list sequentially, a TLB searches every sticky note in 1 cycle using parallel associative CAM hardware, and power-of-2 page sizes (2n) turn division/modulo into zero-logic wire slicing!
  • Why Each Mechanism Exists: Hierarchical Paging breaks sparse page tables into demand-allocated sub-tables (until 64-bit depth hits 4+ RAM hops, Slide 17); Hashed Page Tables compact sparse 64-bit lookups; Inverted Page Tables bound table RAM strictly to physical frame count O(RAM) at the cost of making shared memory hard; Segmentation (Slide 17) matches programmer views (code/stack/heap) with variable-length bounds checked by STBR/STLR.

1. The Paging Hardware Model & Bit-Split Math (§9.3.1)

Paging permits a process's physical address space to be completely non-contiguous! Physical memory is divided into fixed-sized blocks called Frames, and logical memory is broken into same-sized blocks called Pages (always a power of 2, typically 4 KB to 1 GB). Because every free frame fits any logical page, External Fragmentation is 0%! Only the last page of a process averages ~50% Internal Fragmentation (half a page).

m-bit Logical Address Space (2m bytes) & Page Size = 2n bytes:
Lower n bits = Page Offset (d)  |  Upper (m − n) bits = Page Number (p)
Page Table Entries = 2m−n  |  Physical Address = (Frame f × 2n) + d
🧮 Exam Calculations: Slide 17 Sample Q1, Sample Q2, Internal Frag & Decimal Paging
  • Binary Bit-Split: Suppose a system has a 32-bit logical address space (4 GB) and 4 KB page size (4 KB = 4096 = 212 bytes).
    ⇒ Offset d takes 12 bits; Page Number p takes 32 − 12 = 20 bits (meaning up to 220 = 1,048,576 pages per process!). (Similarly on 8-bit Slide 17 trace: m=8, frame=4B=22 ⇒ LA=7 = 000001|11 gives p=1, d=3.)
  • Decimal Translation: Page Size = 4 bytes, Page Table maps P0→F5, P1→F6, P2→F1, P3→F2, Logical Address = 13: p = 13/4 = 3, d = 13%4 = 1, PageTable[3] ⇒ f = 2, so PA = (2 × 4) + 1 = 9! (Slide 17 also traces LA=2 ('c') → p=0, d=2 → F5 → PA=22.)
  • Slide 17 Internal Frag & Sample Q1/Q2 (Ex 9.4 & 9.7): With 2,048 B pages and 72,766 B process: 35 pages + 1,086 B ⇒ 2,048 − 1,086 = 962 B internal frag (watch slide 17 typo printing 2^11 (1024)—2^11 is 2048!). Sample Q1: 64 pages (6b) × 1024 B (10b) = 16-bit LA; 32 frames (5b) + 10b = 15-bit PA. Sample Q2 (1 KB = 1024 B): 3085 → (3, 13), 42095 → (41, 111), 215201 → (210, 161), 650000 → (634, 784), 2000001 → (1953, 129).

2. Hardware Support: Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) & EAT (§9.3.2)

Because the Page Table resides in main memory (pointed to by the CPU's PTBR — Page-Table Base Register), every memory read/write naively requires two RAM accesses (1 to fetch frame f from Page Table, 1 for the actual data byte—cutting speed in half!). Hardware fixes this with a high-speed associative cache called the TLB (typically 32–1,024 entries searched in parallel in ~1 CPU cycle):

CPU ──(p, d)──> [ TLB Associative Lookup ] ├── HIT (α) ──> yields Frame f immediately ──> Physical (f, d) in RAM (Time: TLB + Mem) └── MISS (1-α) ──> reads PageTable[p] in RAM & updates TLB ──> Physical (f, d) (Time: TLB + 2×Mem)
  • ASIDs (Address-Space Identifiers): Tagging each TLB entry with the process's ASID prevents flushing the entire TLB on every context switch, while still blocking process A from accessing process B's translations.
  • Protection & Shared Pages (§9.3.3–§9.3.4): Each Page Table Entry (PTE) stores Valid-Invalid bit (v=in logical address space, i=illegal access trap) plus R/W/X protection bits. Reentrant read-only code (e.g., 40 users running libc or text editor) maps different processes' PTEs to the same physical frames!
🧮 Exam Calculation 2: Effective Access Time (EAT) with TLB
EAT = α · (TLB + Mem) + (1 − α) · (TLB + 2 · Mem) Note: Silberschatz 10th Ed. §9.3.2.1 uses 10 ns RAM with parallel TLB (≈ 0 ns), simplifying to α(10) + (1−α)(20) = 12 ns at 80% / 10.1 ns at 99%. Always include TLB latency if explicitly specified by the problem!
Worked Numerical Problem (with explicit 20 ns TLB): Assume TLB lookup = 20 ns, Main Memory access = 100 ns.
• At 80% Hit Ratio (α = 0.80): EAT = 0.80(20 + 100) + 0.20(20 + 200) = 96 + 44 = 140 ns (40% slowdown over 100 ns).
• At 99% Hit Ratio (α = 0.99): EAT = 0.99(120) + 0.01(220) = 118.8 + 2.2 = 121 ns (only 21% overhead!).

3. Page Table Structures (§9.4) & Segmentation (Slide 17)

With 32-bit addresses and 4 KB pages, 220 entries × 4 B = 4 MB per process! Worse, with 64-bit addresses (252 entries!), a flat contiguous page table per process is astronomically impossible. Three 10th Ed. §9.4 solutions—plus Hardware Segmentation from Slide 17—exist:

Structure (§9.4 / Slide 17)How It WorksPros & Cons (64-Bit Verdict)
1. Hierarchical (Multi-Level, §9.4.1)Pages the page table itself! E.g., 32-bit splits into p1 (10b) | p2 (10b) | d (12b). Only active inner tables allocated in RAM.Works great for 32-bit (2 levels). FAILS on 64-bit: needs 4–7 levels → up to 4–7 RAM hops on a TLB miss!
2. Hashed Page Tables (§9.4.2)Hashes virtual page number p into a bucket chain; compares p along linked list elements (Clustered stores 16 consecutive pages/node).Excellent for sparse 64-bit address spaces (>32 bits).
3. Inverted Page Table (§9.4.3)ONE global table for the entire OS with exactly 1 slot per physical frame (entry = <pid, page_num>)! Indexed by frame f.Slashes page-table RAM drastically regardless of process count. Cons: Lookup requires searching (needs hash table); makes shared memory hard (1 frame maps 1 <pid, p>!).
4. Segmentation (Slide 17)Logical address is <segment-number s, offset d> mapped through Segment Table (base, limit) pointed to by STBR & STLR; traps unless s < STLR and 0 ≤ d < limit.Matches programmer view (code/stack/data) & per-segment protection, yet re-introduces variable-size external fragmentation!

deck_18.html:
DECK 18 · VIRTUAL MEMORY & PAGER · SILBERSCHATZ CH. 10 (§10.1–§10.6)

Virtual Memory, Demand Paging, Copy-on-Write, Page Replacement & Thrashing

Silberschatz 10th Ed. Chapter 10 (§10.1–§10.6) · CPCS-361 Final Exam Flagship Topic
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Trace all 6 hardware/OS steps of handling a Page Fault (§10.2.1).
  • Compute Demand Paging Effective Access Time (EAT) showing why page-fault rate p must stay tiny (§10.2.3).
  • Explain Copy-on-Write (CoW) optimization during fork() (§10.3.1).
  • Hand-trace FIFO, Optimal (OPT), LRU, Second-Chance (Clock), and Enhanced Clock page replacement (§10.4).
  • Demonstrate Belady's Anomaly and explain the Stack Property (§10.4.2–§10.4.4).
  • Analyze Frame Allocation (Equal/Proportional, incl. Slide 18 m=62 free frames), Thrashing, the Working-Set Model, and Page-Fault Frequency (PFF) (§10.5–§10.6).
💡 Intuition First: Desk vs. Basement Archive & The Thrashing Cliff
  • Naive Solutions → Visible Failure: Preloading every byte of a binary wastes RAM on error handlers that never run; conversely, cramming too many runnable processes until Σ WSSi > m flips the OS into Thrashing (§10.6.1): every process steals frames from peers, CPU utilization nosedives toward 0% waiting on swap, and a naive scheduler admits even more jobs thinking the CPU is idle! Meanwhile FIFO isn't even monotonic—giving 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 a 4th frame increases faults from 9 to 10 (Belady's Anomaly)!
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: Treat RAM as a small study desk (m frames) beside a slow basement file room (swap): keep only today's active locality on the desk and fetch missing sheets on demand (page fault). Copy-on-Write (§10.3.1) lets forked siblings share one clean textbook until someone writes a margin note—copying only that single edited page. Where the analogy breaks: Desk clutter degrades gradually, whereas virtual memory suffers a sudden 40× cliff even at p = 0.001 (8 ms disk vs 200 ns RAM), and real CPUs cannot reorder hardware LRU stacks on every memory load so they run a Clock sweep ((0,0) clean-unused evicted before (0,1) dirty victims needing two disk trips!).
  • Why Each Formula Exists: EAT = (1−p)·ma + p·page_fault_time (§10.2.3) proves p must stay below ~1 in 400,000 for ≤10% slowdown; Working-Set D = Σ WSSi and PFF throttle multiprogramming directly before thrashing starts.

1. Demand Paging & The 6-Step Page Fault Sequence (§10.2)

Virtual memory separates the programmer's huge logical view (e.g., stacks/heaps separated by gigabytes of sparse empty space) from limited physical RAM. With Demand Paging (a lazy pager), pages are loaded from disk only when actually referenced! Each PTE carries a Valid-Invalid bit: v = in RAM; i = either illegal address OR valid page still on disk.

⚠️ Memorize All 6 Steps of Handling a Page Fault (Silberschatz Fig. 10.5)
  1. Step 1 (Trap): Reference to page marks PTE bit = i (invalid) ⇒ MMU hardware raises a Page-Fault Trap to the OS.
  2. Step 2 (PCB Validation): Kernel checks an internal process table: if the memory reference is truly illegal (segfault), terminate process; if valid but on disk, proceed to page it in.
  3. Step 3 (Free Frame): OS locates a free physical frame from the free-frame list (if none, runs Page Replacement to evict a victim!).
  4. Step 4 (Disk Read): OS schedules disk controller I/O to read the desired page into the newly allocated frame (process enters Waiting state while disk runs).
  5. Step 5 (Update Tables): Upon disk interrupt completion, OS modifies the internal table and sets the PTE's frame number + flips bit i → v.
  6. Step 6 (Restart Instruction): OS reschedules the process and restarts the exact trapped machine instruction—now the PTE is valid and execution resumes seamlessly!
🧮 Exam Calculation: Demand Paging EAT (Showing Sensitivity to p)
EAT = (1 − p) × ma + p × page_fault_time page_fault_time includes: fault trap overhead + swap-out dirty victim (if needed) + swap-in desired page + restart overhead.

Worked Problem: Memory access time ma = 200 ns, average page-fault service time = 8 ms = 8,000,000 ns, and 1 fault out of 1,000 accesses (p = 0.001):

EAT = (1 − 0.001) × 200 + 0.001 × 8,000,000 = 199.8 + 8,000 = 8,199.8 ns (≈ 8.2 μs!)
That single 0.1% fault rate causes a ~41× slowdown (8,199.8 / 200 = 40.999; Silberschatz §10.2.3 rounds to "a factor of 40"!). To keep performance degradation under 10% (EAT ≤ 220 ns), we need p < 0.0000025 (fewer than 1 fault in ~400,000 accesses)!

2. Copy-on-Write (CoW — §10.3.1)

Naively copying every parent page on fork() is wasteful when the child immediately calls exec()! With Copy-on-Write, parent and child initially share the exact same physical frames, marked read-only. Only if either process attempts to write to a shared page does hardware trap, causing the OS to duplicate just that one modified page cleanly.

3. Page Replacement Algorithms & Belady's Anomaly (§10.4)

Notice the Modify (Dirty) Bit optimization: if an evicted victim frame has dirty == 0, it matches disk identically—so OS skips writing it back to swap, saving 50% of page-fault disk I/O!

Compare algorithms using Silberschatz §10.4.1's 20-page reference string with 3 physical frames: 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3, 2, 1, 2, 0, 1, 7, 0, 1 (Slide 18 note: Lecture Slide 18 inserts an extra 0, 3 mid-string making 22 references—both strings yield identical totals: FIFO = 15, OPT = 9, LRU = 12!):

AlgorithmEviction PolicyFaults (3 Frames)Notes & Belady Check
FIFOEvicts the page brought into RAM earliest (oldest arrival).15 faultsSimple queue, ignores usage! SUFFERS BELADY'S ANOMALY!
Optimal (OPT / MIN)Evicts the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future.9 faultsProvably lowest faults! Impossible to implement live (requires future knowledge); used as theoretical benchmark.
LRUEvicts the page unused for the longest time in the past.12 faultsExcellent! A Stack Algorithm (frames with k ⊂ frames with k+1) ⇒ immune to Belady's Anomaly. Hardware approximates via counters or stack.
Second-Chance (Clock)Circular FIFO pointer + 1 Reference Bit: if ref==0, evict; if ref==1, clear ref=0, advance clock!~12–14 faultsStandard real-OS hardware approximation (used in Linux/UNIX variants). Enhanced Clock uses (ref, dirty) ordered classes: (0,0) → (0,1) → (1,0) → (1,1).
🧮 Proof Trace: Belady's Anomaly on FIFO (String: 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

Counterintuitively, adding MORE physical frames under FIFO can INCREASE page faults!
• With 3 Frames: Total = 9 page faults.
• With 4 Frames: 1(F), 2(F), 3(F), 4(F), 1(hit), 2(hit), 5(F replaces 1), 1(F replaces 2), 2(F replaces 3), 3(F replaces 4), 4(F replaces 5), 5(F replaces 1) ⇒ Total = 10 page faults!
Why? FIFO lacks the Stack Property, whereas OPT and LRU satisfy the inclusion property where pages in RAM for n frames are always a strict subset of pages in RAM for n+1 frames.

4. Frame Allocation, Thrashing & Working-Set Model (§10.5–§10.6)

  • Frame Allocation (§10.5.2): Each process requires a strict architecture minimum (enough frames to complete a single complex assembly instruction with indirect operands). Allocation splits frames across processes via Equal Allocation (m / n, Slide 18 e.g. 100 / 5 = 20) or Proportional Allocation ((si / S) × m; e.g., in Silberschatz §10.5.2 with m = 64 total where 2 are OS-reserved leaving 62 free user frames and sizes s1=10, s2=127, they get 4 and 57 frames!). Global Replacement lets a process steal frames from others (higher throughput, variable speed); Local Replacement restricts eviction to a process's own frames (predictable).
  • Thrashing (§10.6): When a process holds fewer frames than its active locality needs, it page-faults constantly, replacing a page it needs back within microseconds! As OS sees low CPU utilization (processes stuck waiting on paging disk), the scheduler foolishly swaps in even more processes, shrinking each process's frames further—causing CPU utilization to plummet toward 0% while disk swaps continuously!
  • Two Remedies Against Thrashing:
    1. Working-Set Model (Denning): Tracks the set of unique pages referenced in the last Δ memory references (Working Set WSSi). Total frame demand is D = Σ WSSi. If D > m (total physical frames), suspend a process and swap it out until frames free!
    2. Page-Fault Frequency (PFF): Sets upper and lower bounds on each process's actual page-fault rate: if faults exceed the upper bound, allocate an extra frame; if below the lower bound, reclaim a frame.

deck_19.html:
DECK 19 · MASS STORAGE & RAID · SILBERSCHATZ CH. 11 (§11.1–§11.3, §11.8)

HDD & NVM Flash Structure, Disk Scheduling Algorithms & RAID Levels

Silberschatz 10th Ed. Chapter 11 (§11.1–§11.3, §11.8) & Lecture Slide 19 · CPCS-361 Final Exam Core Numerical Traces
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Describe magnetic HDD geometry (Platters, Tracks, Sectors, Cylinders) and compute Seek + Rotational + Transfer Latency (§11.1.1).
  • Contrast HDDs with NVM / NAND Flash SSDs (erase blocks, FTL, garbage collection, write amplification, wear leveling, FIFO/NOOP scheduling) (§11.1.2, §11.3).
  • Compute exact head-movement totals for FCFS, SCAN, C-SCAN (§11.2.1–§11.2.3) plus Slide 19's SSTF, LOOK, C-LOOK and 0..4999 Review Problem.
  • Compare all standard RAID Levels (0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 0+1, 1+0) on capacity, fault tolerance, and small-write penalties (§11.8).
💡 Intuition First: Skyscraper Elevators, One-Way Ski Lifts & Non-Overwritable Flash
  • Naive Solutions → Visible Failure: Serving disk cylinders strictly FCFS swings the mechanical arm wildly (7,037 cylinders on Slide 19's Review Problem vs 1,745 under SSTF!). Greedily chasing the nearest track (SSTF) slashes seeks yet can starve far-edge tracks forever. Conversely, applying mechanical elevator sorting to an NVMe SSD burns CPU time for zero gain while ignoring flash's real trap: NAND pages cannot overwrite in place!
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: An HDD head arm is a 5,000-floor freight elevator: SCAN rides all the way to the roof/basement (0..199 or 0..4999); C-SCAN acts like a one-way ski lift so edge floors never wait double turns; LOOK/C-LOOK stop at the highest/lowest waiting button instead of riding to an empty roof! RAID mirrors twin notebooks (RAID 1), deals cards across drives (RAID 0), or keeps algebraic XOR receipts (RAID 5). Where the analogy breaks: Flash SSDs have zero moving arms—they work like chalkboards where erasing requires wiping an entire big grid (Erase Block) to fresh space, driven by the controller's FTL and Wear Leveling (§11.1.2).
  • Why Each Formula Exists: 0.5 × (60 / RPM) captures the average half-circle spin wait (e.g., 4.17 ms at 7,200 RPM); N, N/2, N−1, N−2 capture exact usable space vs. surviving 0, 1, or 2 dead drives (§11.8.3).

1. HDD Physical Geometry vs. NVM Solid-State Drives (§11.1)

  • Magnetic Hard Disks (HDDs): Composed of spinning platters covered in magnetic tracks subdivided into 512B/4KB sectors. The set of identical-radius tracks stacked across all surfaces forms a Cylinder. Total positioning delay = Seek Time (moving arm assembly to target cylinder, ~3–12 ms) + Rotational Latency (waiting for target sector to spin under head; average = ½ full rotation, e.g., 7,200 RPM = 8.33 ms/rev ⇒ 4.17 ms avg rotational latency!).
  • Nonvolatile Memory (NVM / NAND Flash SSDs): Zero moving mechanical heads (→ ~50–100 μs random access, silent, shockproof). Key Hardware Constraints: Reads/writes occur per Page (e.g., 4 KB), BUT NAND cannot overwrite in place—an entire large Erase Block (~128–512 KB) must be erased before rewriting! Because flash cells wear out after finite Program/Erase (P/E) cycles, the controller's Flash Translation Layer (FTL) implements garbage collection, Wear Leveling (spreading writes across physical blocks evenly), and over-provisioning to combat Write Amplification.

2. Disk Head Scheduling Algorithms & Complete Worked Trace (§11.2 & Slide 19)

Because HDD seek distance dominates latency, the OS orders pending I/O cylinder requests cleanly. (Note: On SSDs, head movement doesn't exist, so simpler FCFS/NOOP FIFO queues excel—§11.3!). Edition Note: Silberschatz 10th Ed. §11.2 covers FCFS (§11.2.1), SCAN (§11.2.2), and C-SCAN (§11.2.3), while Slide 19 also tests SSTF, LOOK, and C-LOOK. Let's trace the famous Silberschatz Ch. 11 dataset:

Disk Geometry: Cylinders 0 to 199  |  Initial Head Position: 53 (previously moved downward toward 0 or upward—watch direction note!)  |  Request Queue: 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67

AlgorithmService Order from Head = 53Step-by-Step DistanceTotal Head Movement
FCFS53 → 98 → 183 → 37 → 122 → 14 → 124 → 65 → 6745 + 85 + 146 + 85 + 108 + 110 + 59 + 2640 cylinders (wild swings!)
SSTF
(Shortest Seek Time First)		53 → 65 → 67 → 37 → 14 → 98 → 122 → 124 → 183
(Picks nearest next request greedily; tie 53→65 vs 37 is 12 vs 16)		12 + 2 + 30 + 23 + 84 + 24 + 2 + 59236 cylinders
(Warning: Can STARVE distant edge tracks!)
SCAN
(Elevator — moving toward 0 first)		53 → 37 → 14 → 0 → 65 → 67 → 98 → 122 → 124 → 183
(Sweeps ALL the way to end cylinder 0, then reverses!)		(53 − 0) + (183 − 0) = 53 + 183236 cylinders
(Note: If moving UP toward 199 first: 53→199→14 = 146+185 = 331!)
C-SCAN
(Circular SCAN — moving UP toward 199)		53 → 65 → 67 → 98 → 122 → 124 → 183 → 199 → 0 → 14 → 37
(Treats disk as circular loop; zero servicing on 199→0 return!)		(199 − 53) + (199 − 0) + (37 − 0) = 146 + 199 + 37382 cylinders
(Gives much more uniform wait time than SCAN!)
LOOK
(Moving DOWN toward 0 first)		53 → 37 → 14 → 65 → 67 → 98 → 122 → 124 → 183
(Like SCAN, but reverses at last request 14—skips empty 14→0!)		(53 − 14) + (183 − 14) = 39 + 169208 cylinders
C-LOOK
(Moving UP toward 199 first)		53 → 65 → 67 → 98 → 122 → 124 → 183 → 14 → 37
(Jumps directly from highest request 183 to lowest request 14!)		(183 − 53) + (183 − 14) + (37 − 14) = 130 + 169 + 23322 cylinders

Exam Tip & Slide 19 Review Problem: Always verify whether the prompt includes the full-sweep return jump 199 → 0 in total C-SCAN head movement! Silberschatz explicitly counts 199 cylinders for that return sweep (hence 146 + 199 + 37 = 382, and 183 − 14 = 169 in C-LOOK). Also watch a known Slide 19 typo printing SCAN = 208 (208 is actually LOOK without reaching 0; hitting 0 gives 236!). Slide 19 Review Question (0..4999, curr=143, prev=125 moving UP; queue 130, 1750, 1022, 1509, 948, 1774, 913, 1470, 86): FCFS = 7,037, SSTF = 1,745, SCAN(to 4999) = 9,769, LOOK(to 1774) = 3,319, C-LOOK = 3,363 (1,675 excluding flyback).

3. RAID Levels (Redundant Arrays of Independent Disks — §11.8)

RAID combines multiple physical drives for two goals: Reliability via Redundancy (surviving disk failure) and Performance via Striping (splitting data blocks across drives in parallel):

RAID LevelTechniqueUsable Space (N Disks)Fault Tolerance & Key Trade-Off
RAID 0Non-redundant Block StripingN disks (100%)ZERO redundancy! Losing 1 drive destroys the whole array. Max speed/space.
RAID 1Disk MirroringN / 2 disks (50%)Survives 1 failure per mirror pair. Fastest reads (dual heads), 2× disk cost.
RAID 4Block Striping + 1 Dedicated Parity DiskN − 1 disksSurvives 1 failure, but the single parity disk becomes a severe write bottleneck!
RAID 5Block Striping + Distributed Parity (XOR) across all N drivesN − 1 disksSurvives 1 drive failure. Eliminates RAID 4 parity bottleneck; small random write requires 4 I/Os (read old data+parity, write new data+parity).
RAID 6Block Striping + Dual Distributed Parity (P+Q Reed-Solomon)N − 2 disksSurvives 2 simultaneous drive failures! Essential for massive modern TB arrays where a 2nd drive often fails during rebuild.
RAID 1+0 (10) vs 0+1Nested Striping + MirroringN / 2 disks (50%)RAID 1+0 (Stripe of Mirrors) beats RAID 0+1 (Mirror of Stripes)! Why? If 1 drive fails in RAID 0+1, an entire half-stripe degrades and losing ANY drive in the other half kills the array; RAID 1+0 tolerates losing 1 drive from every mirror pair!

deck_20.html:
DECK 20 · FILE SYSTEMS & STORAGE ALLOCATION · SILBERSCHATZ CH. 13, 14 & 15

File System Interface, Directories, Allocation Methods, UNIX Inodes & Free Space

Silberschatz 10th Ed. Chapters 13, 14 & 15 (§13.1–§13.4, §14.1–§14.7, §15.5) · CPCS-361 Final Exam Core
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Identify core File Attributes, Operations, Open-File Tables (per-process vs. system-wide), Access Methods (§13.1–§13.2), and UNIX rwx octal protection (§13.4 / Slide 20).
  • Compare the 5 Directory Structures (Single-Level, Two-Level, Tree, Acyclic Graph hard/soft links, General Graph) (§13.3).
  • Trace File-System Layers (§14.1) and the Virtual File System (VFS) interface (§15.5).
  • Compare Contiguous (with Q/R mapping & Extents), Linked (FAT), and Indexed Allocation (§14.4).
  • Calculate maximum file capacity in the UNIX Multi-Level Inode Scheme (§14.4.3).
  • Master Free-Space Management (Bit Vector formula, Linked List, Grouping, Counting), Unified Buffer Cache (§14.6.2), and Journaling (§14.5–§14.7).
💡 Intuition First: Tiered Shipping Manifests, Write-Ahead Ledgers & Universal Plugs
  • Naive Designs → Visible Failure: Laying every file strictly contiguous on disk suffers external fragmentation and freezes file growth without full copies (§14.4.1). Pure linked lists cure fragmentation yet force slow O(N) pointer hops on random seeks—and 1 flipped sector loses the whole file tail! Updating metadata directly in-place crashes into hours-long full-disk fsck scans, and keeping un-unified Buffer + Page caches stores two conflicting copies of mmap()-ed files (§14.6.2)!
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: A UNIX Inode (§14.4.3) is a tiered shipping manifest: 12 direct tracking numbers on page 1 for tiny files (1 hop!), plus single/double/triple nested binders stretching past 4 TB! VFS (§15.5) is a standardized wall socket (vnode) letting one read() syscall drive ext4, NTFS, or network NFS seamlessly. Journaling (§14.7.2) logs receipts in an append-only notebook before touching the main ledger. Where analogies break: Unlike human file folders, allowing general cyclic links breaks simple reference-count deletion (requiring garbage collection, §13.3.5).
  • Why Each Formula Exists: Contiguous Q = LA / 512, Block = Start + Q, offset = R gives zero-lookup O(1) disk arithmetic (Slide 20); Bit Vector word*w + bit uses <0.003% RAM (32 MB for 1 TB) to locate free runs in a single CPU bit-scan instruction (§14.5.1).

1. File Concept, Open-File Tables & Directory Structures (Ch. 13)

A File is a named collection of related information recorded on secondary storage. Its metadata (name, unique identifier number, type, disk location, size, protection, timestamps) lives in directory entries and the disk's File Control Block (FCB / UNIX Inode). To avoid searching directories on every read()/write(), open() loads metadata into two kernel tables:

  • Per-Process Open-File Table: Tracks process-specific state (current file-position pointer, access mode R/W, pointer to system-wide entry) indexed by File Descriptor (FD).
  • System-Wide Open-File Table: Holds process-independent FCB metadata (file size, disk block pointers, dates, and an Open Count so deleting/closing only destroys the file once open_count == 0).

Directory Structures & Protection (§13.3–§13.4): Single-Level (name collisions across users) → Two-Level (one directory per user, isolates names) → Tree-Structured (subdirectories, absolute vs. relative paths) → Acyclic-Graph (permits shared files/dirs via Hard Links sharing the same Inode + reference count vs. Symbolic/Soft Links holding a pathname string; watch out for dangling pointers!) → General Graph (cycles possible, needs garbage-collection cycle detection). UNIX File Protection (§13.4 / Slide 20): 3-bit octals for owner / group / public—e.g., chmod 761 game sets owner=111 (rwx), group=110 (rw-), public=001 (--x), paired with chgrp G game.

2. File System Layers (§14.1) & Virtual File System (VFS — §15.5)

Application → Logical File System (Dirs, FCB/Inode, Protection) → [ VFS Interface (§15.5 uniform vnode abstraction over ext4, NTFS, NFS) ] → File-Organization Module (maps Logical Block # → Physical Disk Block #, Free Space) → Basic File System & I/O Control (Device Drivers + Buffer Cache) → Hardware Disk

3. Disk Space Allocation Methods Compared (§14.4)

MethodMechanismSequential & Random AccessKey Pros & Cons
1. ContiguousFile occupies consecutive disk blocks [start, length]. (Slide 20 with 512 B blocks: Q = LA / 512, DiskBlk = Start + Q, byte offset = R = LA % 512.)Sequential: Fastest!
Direct/Random: O(1) (start + i).		Suffers External Fragmentation & hard to grow a file without copying! (Modern Extents like Veritas allocate contiguous chunks linked together to cure this!).
2. Linked AllocationEach block holds a pointer to the next block (file = linked list anywhere; clustering groups multiple blocks per pointer to shrink pointer overhead!).Sequential: Good.
Direct/Random: TERRIBLE O(N) (must chase pointers!).		Zero external fragmentation, easy growth. Cons: Pointer overhead (~4B/block) + 1 corrupted pointer loses rest of file.
FAT (File Allocation Table)Linked pointers pulled out of data blocks into a central table on disk cached in RAM!Random access jumps straight through RAM FAT pointers before hitting disk!Simple, zero external fragmentation, fast random seeks (still O(N) pointer walk in RAM, bottlenecked for multi-TB disks).
3. Indexed AllocationPuts all data block pointers into a per-file Index Block.Sequential: Fast.
Direct/Random: O(1)!		Zero external fragmentation! Small files waste most of an index block; huge files outgrow 1 index block (fixed via Multi-Level Index!).

4. UNIX Combined Scheme (Inode) & Max File Size Calculation (§14.4.3)

A UNIX Inode combines direct pointers (zero extra disk hops for tiny files!) with multi-level indirect blocks for gigabyte/terabyte files:

INODE STRUCTURE (Example: 12 Direct + 1 Single Indirect + 1 Double Indirect + 1 Triple Indirect): [ 12 Direct Ptrs ] → Point directly to first 12 Data Blocks [ 1 Single Indir ] → Index Block → P Data Blocks [ 1 Double Indir ] → Outer Index Block → P Inner Index Blocks → P² Data Blocks [ 1 Triple Indir ] → Level-1 → P Level-2 → P² Level-3 → P³ Data Blocks
🧮 Worked Final Exam Problem: Calculate Max File Size for UNIX Inode

Given: Block Size = 4 KB (4,096 B), Disk Block Pointer Size = 4 Bytes, and Inode has 12 Direct, 1 Single Indirect, 1 Double Indirect, 1 Triple Indirect pointer:

  1. Pointers per Index Block (P): 4,096 B / 4 B = 1,024 = 210 pointers.
  2. Direct Capacity: 12 × 4 KB = 48 KB.
  3. Single Indirect: 210 × 4 KB = 1,024 × 4 KB = 4 MB.
  4. Double Indirect: (210)2 × 4 KB = 220 × 4 KB = 4 GB.
  5. Triple Indirect: (210)3 × 4 KB = 230 × 4 KB = 4 TB.
  6. Total Max File Size: 48 KB + 4 MB + 4 GB + 4 TB ≈ 4.004 TB!

5. Free-Space Management & Recovery (§14.5–§14.7)

  • Bit Vector (Bitmap): 1 bit per disk block (1 = free, 0 = allocated, or vice versa). Compact (1 TB disk with 4 KB blocks = 228 bits = only 32 MB bitmap) and fast hardware bit-scan instructions!
    Block # = (Bits_per_word × First_nonempty_word) + First_1_bit_offset (e.g., 32-bit words, word #2 has first 1-bit at offset 5 ⇒ Block 32 × 2 + 5 = 69).
  • Linked Free List: Chains free blocks together using disk pointers (no extra bitmap RAM, slow to find contiguous runs).
  • Grouping: Stores addresses of N free blocks in the first free block; the Nth address points to another block holding N more free addresses.
  • Counting (Run-Length): Stores pairs (first_free_block, count_of_contiguous_free_blocks)—great when contiguous allocation frees/allocates large runs!
  • Journaling (Log-Based File Systems): Writes metadata updates sequentially to a circular Journal Log before modifying disk structures; after a power crash, kernel replays committed journal entries in seconds instead of running an hours-long full-disk fsck!

deck_21.html:
DECK 21 · HARDWARE & KERNEL I/O · SILBERSCHATZ CH. 12 (§12.1–§12.5)

I/O Hardware, Polling vs. Interrupts vs. DMA, Application API & Kernel I/O Subsystem

Silberschatz 10th Ed. Chapter 12 (§12.1–§12.5) · CPCS-361 Final Exam Core
🎯 Master Learning Objectives
  • Trace I/O hardware communication over Ports, Buses, Controllers, and contrast Port-Mapped vs. Memory-Mapped I/O (§12.2–§12.2.1).
  • Compare all 3 Hardware I/O Transfer Mechanisms: Polling (PIO), Interrupt-Driven I/O, and DMA (6-step transfer cycle, Fig. 12.6) (§12.2.2–§12.2.4).
  • Classify OS Device Abstractions (Block vs. Character, Network, Clock) and Blocking vs. Nonblocking vs. Asynchronous I/O plus vectored readv() (§12.3.4–§12.3.5, Fig. 12.9).
  • Master Kernel I/O Subsystem services: I/O Scheduling (Device-status table Fig. 12.10), Buffering (Single/Double/Circular), Caching vs. Buffering, and Spooling (§12.4–§12.5).
💡 Intuition First: Mailroom Doorbells, Freight Assistants & Copy Isolation
  • Naive Solutions → Visible Failure: Checking while (status.busy); spins a GHz CPU core uselessly waiting milliseconds for a keyboard/disk (§12.2.2); raising an interrupt for every single byte during a 10 GB copy saturates CPU trap handlers (§12.2.4); issuing async writes directly out of a user's live array lets the app mutate buffer bytes mid-DMA!
  • Mental Model + Where It Breaks: Picture the CPU as a busy executive and the disk controller as a distant mailroom: Polling means walking to the mailroom every microsecond; Interrupts (§12.2.3) install an IRQ doorbell checked between instructions; DMA (§12.2.4, Fig. 12.6) hands one signed work order (command block) to an assistant who wheels the whole crate directly into RAM (cycle stealing) and rings the doorbell once when done! Where the analogy breaks: Unlike human assistants stopping the boss, DMA cycle-stealing borrows RAM bus cycles while the CPU keeps computing inside registers and L1/L2 caches!
  • Why Each Distinction Exists: Buffer vs. Cache (§12.4.3): a Buffer may hold the only live copy of in-flight data, whereas a Cache always copies data safely backed elsewhere; Double Buffering (Slide 21 / §12.4.2): separates Kernel DMA buffer from User buffer via two copies so app writes never corrupt outbound DMA.

1. I/O Hardware & Controller Registers (§12.2–§12.2.1)

Devices communicate via a Port (connection point), shared Bus (PCIe/SATA daisy chain), and Device Controller electronics containing 4 internal registers:

  • Data-in Register (host reads from device) & Data-out Register (host writes to device).
  • Status Register (bits: busy, command-ready, data-available, error).
  • Control Register (CPU writes commands: start read, change parity, seek).

Port-Mapped vs. Memory-Mapped I/O (§12.2.1): Legacy Port-Mapped I/O uses dedicated CPU instructions (IN/OUT). Memory-Mapped I/O maps device registers into the standard physical RAM address space (great for high-bandwidth GPUs/NVMe—regular store instructions write straight into frame buffers, protected by virtual-memory page tables!).

2. Polling vs. Interrupt-Driven I/O vs. DMA (§12.2.2–§12.2.4)

Transfer ModeHardware MechanismWhen Best vs. Worst
1. Polling (Programmed I/O)CPU repeatedly spins checking while (status.busy) ; until device clears busy bit.Best when devices respond in nanoseconds (faster than paying interrupt+context-switch penalty!). Terrible on slow disks/keyboards (wastes 100% CPU!).
2. Interrupt-Driven I/OCPU executes user jobs until controller asserts Interrupt-Request Line; CPU jumps via IVT to ISR, handles byte/status, returns. Includes Nonmaskable (NMI) for critical hardware errors and Maskable (disabled during critical kernel sections) + Interrupt Chaining for shared vectors.Efficient for slow/moderate sporadic I/O (mouse, keyboard, timers). Still burns excessive CPU interrupts if transferring gigabytes byte-by-byte!
3. Direct Memory Access (DMA)Dedicated DMA Controller (or DVMA on virtual-address IOMMU systems) moves entire memory blocks directly between controller buffer and RAM via bus cycle stealing without involving the CPU for each byte!Mandatory for high-bandwidth disks, NICs, GPUs! Drops interrupt rate by 4,096× (1 interrupt per 4 KB block instead of 4,096 interrupts!).
🧮 Memorize the 6-Step DMA Transfer Cycle (Silberschatz Fig. 12.6)
  1. Device driver instructs disk controller to transfer disk data to a RAM buffer at address X.
  2. Disk controller initiates DMA transfer (or CPU writes target RAM address, direction, and byte count into DMA controller registers).
  3. Disk controller sends each byte/word to the DMA Controller.
  4. DMA controller cycle-steals the memory bus from the CPU (pausing CPU memory bus accesses briefly, never CPU cache work!) and writes bytes straight into RAM starting at X, incrementing address & decrementing byte counter.
  5. When byte_count == 0, DMA controller raises ONE single hardware interrupt to signal the CPU!
  6. CPU interrupt handler checks status, moves blocked waiting process to Ready queue, and exits ISR.

3. Application I/O Interface (§12.3.4–§12.3.5, Fig. 12.9)

  • Block Devices (HDD, SSD, USB): Read/write fixed blocks (512B–4KB), support direct random seeking (read/write/seek), and memory-mapped access.
  • Character Stream Devices (Keyboard, Mouse, Serial Port): Send/receive unaddressed byte streams (get/put) without seeking; OSes also expose ioctl() for device-specific escape controls and vectored readv()/writev() scatter-gather (§12.3.5; note Slide 21 typos this as readve()).
  • Blocking vs. Nonblocking vs. Asynchronous I/O (§12.3.4, Fig. 12.9):
    • Blocking: Calling thread suspends (Waiting queue) until I/O finishes.
    • Nonblocking: Call returns immediately with whatever bytes are currently ready (or 0 / EAGAIN), often paired with select() polling multiple FDs.
    • Asynchronous: Call returns immediately so app keeps working while the kernel completes the entire I/O in the background and notifies via signal/callback when done!

4. Kernel I/O Subsystem (§12.4–§12.5)

Kernel I/O ServiceTextbook Mechanism & Purpose
I/O Scheduling (§12.4.1)Reorders per-device wait queues tracked inside the kernel's Device-Status Table (Fig. 12.10) (routing disk queues through §11.2 schedulers) to boost aggregate throughput and fairness.
Buffering (§12.4.2)Memory area storing data in transit between two devices/app to handle (1) speed mismatch (modem vs SSD), (2) transfer-size mismatch (network packet reassembly), and (3) copy semantics (snapshot user buffer in kernel space before async disk write so app changes won't corrupt write!). Double Buffering keeps two separate copies (Kernel buffer + User buffer, Slide 21) so DMA fills cleanly while userspace reads/modifies safely!
Caching vs. BufferingCRITICAL EXAM DISTINCTION: A Buffer may hold the only existing copy of a data item in transit; a Cache strictly holds a faster temporary copy of data that safely resides elsewhere!
Spooling & ReservationSpool (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line): Intermediate disk queue intercepting output for non-sharable sequential devices (printers) so multiple jobs appear to print concurrently without interleaving lines!
I/O ProtectionALL I/O instructions are privileged (Kernel Mode only); users access devices exclusively through validated OS system calls.

ACL (§17.6.2): Column-based (per Object) → Fast revocation | Capability (§17.6.3): Row-based (per Domain) → O(1) check, Hard revocation
