GLOSSARY_DATA.def: A column-wise implementation of the Access Matrix stored with each object listing every domain/user and its allowed rights (supports instant selective revocation).
A protection model where rows represent domains, columns represent objects, and entries represent access rights (read, write, execute, copy, owner).
Mapping program symbolic addresses to physical RAM addresses at Compile time (absolute), Load time (relocatable), or Execution time (MMU dynamic relocation).
A process tag stored inside each TLB entry preventing unnecessary TLB flushes on context switches while isolating process address translations.
A technique of gradually increasing the priority of processes that wait in the system for a long time to prevent starvation.
Formula Speedup <= 1 / (S + (1 - S)/N) proving that the strictly serial portion S of an algorithm caps parallel speedup regardless of core count N.
A multiprocessor architecture where each processor is assigned a specific task, often with a master processor controlling slave processors.
An I/O model where the syscall returns immediately so execution continues, and the kernel notifies the caller only after the entire I/O operation completes.
An operation that completes in its entirety without interruption or cannot be observed in an intermediate state.
Hardware-assisted variable (e.g., atomic_t) supporting uninterruptible read-modify-write operations like atomic_inc via Compare-and-Swap without explicit mutexes.
A deadlock avoidance algorithm developed by Edsger Dijkstra that tests for safety by simulating the allocation of predetermined maximum possible amounts of resources.
The phenomenon where increasing the number of page frames allocated to a process results in an increase in the number of page faults (occurs in FIFO page replacement).
A semaphore whose integer value can range only between 0 and 1; used as a mutex lock for mutual exclusion.
Initial firmware code (ROM/EEPROM) executed at power-on that initializes hardware controllers and loads the OS kernel into RAM.
A fixed-capacity circular buffer shared between producer and consumer processes where full and empty buffer conditions must be synchronized.
IPC producer-consumer models (§3.5.1): Unbounded buffer places no limit on capacity (producer never waits); Bounded buffer fixes capacity so producer also blocks when full.
A critical section requirement stating that there must exist a bound on the number of times other processes are allowed to enter their critical sections after a process has made a request.
Storing data in transit in RAM to absorb device speed/size mismatches and preserve copy semantics; double buffering fills one buffer via DMA while CPU processes the other.
A synchronization technique where a process repeatedly executes a tight loop while waiting for a condition to become true, consuming CPU cycles.

Circular LOOK disk scheduling (Slide 19 / 9th Ed. §10.4): services requests in one direction up to the highest request cylinder, then jumps directly to the lowest request cylinder without touching endpoints 0 or Max.
Circular SCAN disk scheduling: sweeps from head to end cylinder (e.g., 199), immediately returns to cylinder 0 without servicing on the return trip, providing uniform wait times.
Copying information in active use from slower storage into a faster, smaller temporary storage layer to reduce access latency.
A row-wise Access Matrix implementation stored per protection domain holding unforgeable `<object, rights>` tokens (fast verification, harder selective revocation).
OS policy (§3.3.2 / Slide 03) where terminating a parent process automatically forces termination of all its children and descendants.
Block devices (HDD/SSD) transfer fixed blocks with random seek (`read/write/seek`); Character devices (keyboard/serial) transmit unaddressed byte streams (`get/put`).
One of the 4 necessary conditions for deadlock, where a closed chain of processes exists such that each process holds at least one resource needed by the next process in the chain.
A dashed directed edge Pi -> Rj in a resource-allocation graph indicating that process Pi may request resource Rj at some time in the future.
Distributed computing model (§1.10.3) separating specialized compute-servers or file-servers that respond to requests generated by client systems.
Circular-queue approximation of LRU using each frame's hardware Reference Bit (`ref=1` gets cleared & spared once; `ref=0` is evicted).
Shuffling memory contents to place all free memory together in one large contiguous block to overcome external fragmentation; only possible with dynamic relocation.
Atomic CPU instruction `CompareAndSwap(&val, expected, new)` that updates `*val` only if `*val == expected`, returning the original value.
Monitor synchronization queue supporting `x.wait()` (releases monitor & sleeps) and `x.signal()` (wakes 1 waiter; no-op if queue empty).
The mechanism of saving the state of the currently executing process and restoring the state of a different process so execution can be resumed later; pure OS overhead.
Storing each file in consecutive disk blocks (`[start, length]`); delivers O(1) random & sequential reads but suffers external fragmentation and growth stiffness.
A phenomenon in FCFS scheduling where short processes get stuck waiting behind one long, CPU-bound process, resulting in lower CPU and device utilization.
Virtual memory optimization after `fork()` where parent and child share physical frames read-only until either writes, copying only modified pages.
A semaphore whose integer value can range over an unrestricted domain; used to control access to a finite number of resource instances.
A segment of code in which a process accesses and modifies shared variables, tables, or files, requiring mutually exclusive execution.
Distributing partitions of a single dataset across multiple cores where every core applies the identical operation concurrently.
A situation in which every process in a set is waiting for an event that can be caused only by another process in the same set.
A virtual memory technique where pages are loaded into physical memory only when they are referenced during execution (lazy swapper).
A classic synchronization problem illustrating the allocation of shared resources (chopsticks) among competing processes (philosophers) without deadlock or starvation.
A hardware feature allowing high-speed I/O controllers to transfer entire blocks of data directly to/from main memory without CPU intervention, generating only one interrupt per block.
The elapsed time required for the short-term dispatcher to stop one process, switch context + user mode, and jump to the next process.

The OS module that gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler, involving context switching, switching to user mode, and jumping to the proper location in the program.
Hardware support providing at least two modes of operation: User Mode (mode bit = 1) and Kernel/Monitor Mode (mode bit = 0) to protect the OS from errant user programs.
Postponing external library linking until runtime via memory stubs so multiple processes share one read-only RAM copy of libraries like libc/DLLs.
Dynamic-priority real-time scheduler prioritizing whichever task has the earliest upcoming deadline (theoretically achieves up to 100% CPU utilization).
The average time required to access a memory location taking into account cache/TLB hit rates and page fault penalties.
System call (typically called in a forked child) that completely overwrites the calling process's address space with a brand-new binary image.
A contiguous chunk of disk blocks; modern file systems (ext4, NTFS) link multiple large extents together to combine contiguous speed with growth flexibility.
A condition where total free memory space exists to satisfy a request, but it is broken into non-contiguous scattered holes.
A simple file system architecture using a table cached in memory containing disk block pointers for fast linked allocation lookups.
Per-file on-disk metadata structure (called an Inode in UNIX) holding permissions, owner, size, timestamps, and pointers to data blocks.
A contiguous memory allocation strategy that allocates the first hole in memory that is large enough for the process.
SSD controller firmware mapping logical block addresses (LBAs) onto physical NAND pages while handling garbage collection, over-provisioning, and wear leveling.
The UNIX system call used to create a new child process which is an exact duplicate of the calling parent process, returning 0 to the child and the child's PID to the parent.
A fixed-size block of physical main memory into which a logical page can be mapped.
A bar chart timeline illustrating a CPU scheduling sequence with process execution intervals and start/completion times.
Hard links are multiple directory names pointing to the exact same Inode (reference-counted); Symbolic (Soft) links store a text path string that can dangle if target deletes.
Page table structure for >32-bit sparse address spaces hashing virtual page number `p` into collision-chained buckets (`Clustered` stores 16 pages/entry).
A deadlock condition where a process is currently holding at least one resource while waiting to acquire additional resources held by other processes.
Storing all disk block pointers of a file inside a dedicated Index Block (or multi-level index), achieving O(1) random access with zero external fragmentation.
UNIX File Control Block storing file metadata plus direct, single-indirect, double-indirect, and triple-indirect block pointers.
Unused memory space internal to an allocated partition or page caused when the allocated block is slightly larger than the requested payload.
A memory table containing the addresses of interrupt service routines (ISRs) indexed by interrupt request numbers.
A page table architecture with one entry for each physical frame of memory rather than each logical page, indexed by frame number.
File system that writes metadata updates first to an append-only transaction Journal Log before applying them on disk, enabling second-scale crash recovery.
A privileged processor execution mode (mode bit 0) in which all machine instructions and physical memory locations are accessible.
A page replacement algorithm that replaces the page that has not been referenced for the longest period of time in the past.
A hardware register that specifies the size or range of the logical address space for a process, used for memory protection.
Queueing theory identity `n = lambda * W` relating average queue occupancy `n`, arrival rate `lambda`, and average waiting time `W`.
Failure state where runnable threads continuously consume CPU retrying conflicting actions (e.g., polite lock-backoff collisions) without making progress.
Modern modular OS kernel pattern (Linux/macOS/Windows) inserting drivers and filesystems dynamically at runtime with full monolithic call speed.
Logical (virtual) addresses are generated by the CPU inside a process's view; Physical addresses are actual hardware addresses sent by the MMU onto the RAM bus.

GLOSSARY_DATA.term: Long-Term vs. Medium-Term vs. Short-Term Scheduler
GLOSSARY_DATA.def: Long-term (job) controls degree of multiprogramming slowly; Medium-term swaps processes in/out to relieve RAM; Short-term (CPU) dispatches a Ready process in milliseconds.
Improved SCAN elevator disk scheduler that reverses head sweep direction as soon as it reaches the final request in the current direction rather than hitting tracks 0 or Max.
Hardware instruction forcing all pending memory loads/stores to become globally visible across CPU cores before subsequent instructions execute.
The hardware device that dynamically maps logical addresses generated by the CPU to physical addresses in RAM.
Assigning device controller registers directly into standard physical RAM address ranges so standard CPU load/store opcodes control I/O devices.
An IPC mechanism that allows processes to communicate and synchronize their actions without sharing variables, using send() and receive() primitives.
OS architecture minimizing kernel code in Ring 0 (IPC, basic scheduling/memory) while running file systems and drivers as isolated user-space processes.
High-level compiler synchronization construct encapsulating shared data and procedures such that at most one thread executes inside the monitor at once.
Architecture placing all core OS subsystems (scheduler, VFS, drivers, network stack) inside a single privileged Ring 0 address space for fast direct calls.
A CPU scheduling algorithm with multiple priority queues that allows processes to move between queues based on their CPU burst characteristics.
The technique of keeping multiple jobs in memory simultaneously so the CPU always has one job to execute, maximizing CPU utilization.
A logical extension of multiprogramming where the CPU switches between jobs so rapidly that users can interact with each program while it runs (response time < 1s).
The fundamental condition that if a process is executing in its critical section, no other process can be executing in its critical section simultaneously.
Multiprocessor topology where accessing DRAM attached to a CPU's local socket is significantly faster than accessing remote socket memory across interconnect.
A still-running child process whose parent terminated before calling wait(); automatically adopted and later reaped by PID 1 (init / systemd).
A hardware trap raised by the MMU when a program attempts to access a page marked invalid (not currently mapped to physical RAM).
A per-process data structure maintained by the OS to map logical page numbers to physical frame numbers.
Dynamic frame-allocation policy that grants extra frames when a process's page-fault rate exceeds an upper threshold and reclaims frames below a lower threshold.
Distributed model (§1.10.4) with no client/server split; all nodes act equally as peers (e.g., Gnutella, Skype) discovering services via central lookup or broadcast.
A classic software algorithm for two processes that solves the critical section problem using shared variables flag[2] and turn.
Busy-waiting I/O transfer loop where CPU repeatedly inspects a device controller's `busy` status bit (efficient only for ultra-fast nanosecond operations).
Real-time lock protocol temporarily boosting a low-priority lock-holder to match the highest waiting thread's priority until it releases the lock.
Scheduling hazard where a high-priority thread stalls waiting on a lock held by a low-priority thread that keeps getting preempted by medium-priority threads.
The kernel data structure representing a process, storing PID, state, PC, CPU registers, scheduling information, memory limits, and I/O status.
Tendency to keep a thread dispatched on the same physical CPU core so its L1/L2 cache lines remain warm (Soft vs. Hard `sched_setaffinity`).
A set of `<object, access-rights>` pairs defining what operations an executing entity may legally perform (switched via CPU Rings or UNIX `setuid`).
A flaw where several processes access and manipulate shared data concurrently and the outcome depends on the particular order in which access takes place.
Redundant Arrays of Independent Disks balancing speed via striping (0), mirroring redundancy (1), distributed single/dual parity (5/6), and nested stripe-of-mirrors (10).
Static-priority real-time scheduler prioritizing periodic tasks inversely by period (`priority = 1/p`); optimal among fixed-priority policies.
A concurrency problem where multiple reader threads can read shared data concurrently, but writer threads require exclusive access.
A directed graph consisting of process vertices, resource vertices, request edges, and assignment edges used to characterize deadlocks.
Enterprise access control tying privileges to organizational Roles rather than individual users, simplifying Least Privilege management.
A preemptive scheduling algorithm designed for time-sharing systems where each ready process is assigned a fixed time slice (quantum).
A system state where there exists a safe execution sequence of processes such that every process can finish with currently available plus held resources.
Appending a unique random string per user before hashing passwords so identical user passwords produce completely different hashes, defeating Rainbow Tables.
Disk head moves back and forth all the way across cylinders `0 <-> Max`, servicing every queued cylinder in its path.
A synchronization tool consisting of an integer value accessed only through two standard atomic operations: wait() (P) and signal() (V).
A scheduling algorithm that associates with each process the length of its next CPU burst, provably yielding the minimum average waiting time.
The preemptive version of SJF where an executing process is preempted if a newly arrived process has a shorter remaining burst time.
Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line: queuing output for exclusive non-sharable devices (e.g., printers) into separate disk files to prevent interleaved job chaos.
Class of page replacement policies (including OPT and LRU) guaranteeing pages held with k frames are always a subset of k+1 frames, preventing Belady's Anomaly.
Condition where a ready process waits indefinitely because higher-priority or shorter jobs continually run ahead of or preempt it (solved in Priority scheduling via Aging).
Temporarily moving an entire idle process (or individual pages in modern OSes) between RAM and disk backing store to increase multiprogramming capacity.
The programmatic interface by which an application requests a service from the operating system kernel.
Distributing distinct functional threads/operations concurrently across multiple CPU cores operating on shared or independent data.
Atomic hardware instruction reading a boolean memory word and unconditionally setting it `true` in a single indivisible cycle.
A condition where a system spends more time servicing page faults and paging than executing actual instructions.
Number of processes that complete execution per unit time: N / (CT_max - AT_min).
A small, fast associative hardware cache that stores recent page-to-frame translations to accelerate memory access.
Hardware raises asynchronous Interrupts (timer/disk); software generates synchronous Traps/Exceptions either by error (divide-by-zero) or intent (`syscall`).
Design merging file-system buffer cache with virtual-memory page cache so memory-mapped files and standard `read()`/`write()` never double-cache pages.
Resource allocation state where no guaranteed Safe Sequence exists; does NOT imply current deadlock, only that deadlock could occur if processes claim Max.
Kernel abstraction layer exposing uniform file syscalls (`open/read/write` via `vnode` interfaces) seamlessly over heterogeneous ext4, NTFS, or NFS backends.
A memory management capability that provides an idealized abstraction of storage, allowing the execution of processes not completely in physical memory.
Simplified single-instance deadlock-detection graph containing only threads with directed edge `Ti -> Tj` whenever `Ti` awaits a resource held by `Tj`.
SSD FTL technique distributing block erasures evenly across all NAND flash blocks so hot sectors do not burn out hardware prematurely.
A model based on the principle of locality that defines the working set as the set of pages referenced by a process in the most recent delta time units.
A memory allocation strategy that allocates the largest available hole to produce the largest leftover hole, but generally performs poorly.
A process that has terminated via exit(), but whose parent has not yet executed wait() to read its termination status, keeping its PCB in the process table.

inlineSabotage.find: Asymmetric Multiprocessing (AMP): Boss-worker model; one master CPU schedules and assigns tasks to worker CPUs. Simpler kernel locking, poorer scaling.
inlineSabotage.corrupt: Asymmetric Multiprocessing (AMP): Peer-to-peer architecture where every processor runs an identical copy of the OS kernel and competes symmetrically on the shared ready queue without a master coordinator.
inlineSabotage.why: Wait—you described SMP (Symmetric Multiprocessing)! In AMP (Asymmetric), ONE master boss CPU controls/schedules all worker CPUs (§1.3).

bugHunts.prompt: One of these four OS fundamentals statements was secretly altered with a textbook bug. Click the flawed statement:
items: 1. Hardware invokes the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) by indexing into the Interrupt Vector Table (IVT) stored in low memory.
2. Multiprogramming focuses on maximizing CPU utilization by switching whenever the active job waits for I/O.
3. During a system call trap, CPU hardware switches the Mode Bit from 0 (User Mode) to 1 (Kernel Mode) so the OS can read user buffers safely.
4. DMA transfers an entire block directly between a device controller buffer and RAM, firing only 1 interrupt per block.
bugHunts.fix: Flipped Mode Bit values! User Mode = Mode Bit 1 (Ring 3) and Kernel Mode = Mode Bit 0 (Ring 0). A trap transitions Mode Bit 1 -> 0, NOT 0 -> 1!

bugHunts.prompt: Find the broken step in this student's Dual-Mode read() syscall trace:
items: Step A: User process runs normal instructions in User Mode (Mode Bit = 1).
Step B: Program triggers trap opcode (SYSCALL) to execute read().
Step C: User program manually sets Mode Bit = 0 in C before indexing the IVT so it runs fast.
Step D: Kernel executes service routine in Ring 0, places result, and executes return-from-trap (Mode Bit 0 -> 1).
bugHunts.fix: Privileged Mode-Bit switching CANNOT be done by user code! Hardware sets Mode Bit -> 0 automatically only as part of the trap instruction itself (§1.4.2).

socratic.q: Pause & Predict: Why can't we use Interrupts alone to kill an accidental user-space `while(1);` infinite loop without a Hardware Timer?
socratic.a: If the user program computes endlessly without requesting I/O or syscalls, no disk/trap interrupt ever arrives from it! Only a programmable hardware Timer counting down clock ticks guarantees periodic Kernel reentry (§1.4.3).

socratic.q: Compare Microkernel vs. Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs): Why does Linux load drivers via LKMs instead of pure user-space microkernel servers?
socratic.a: Pure microkernels pay repeated user <-> kernel IPC message-passing context switches on every syscall/driver call. LKMs preserve modular dynamic loading while calling directly across Ring 0 pointers at monolithic speed (§2.8.4).

inlineSabotage.find: One-to-One (Linux, Windows): Each user thread → 1 kernel thread. True multi-core parallelism + non-blocking on syscall, slight creation overhead.
inlineSabotage.corrupt: One-to-One (Linux, Windows): Multiplexes all user threads onto 1 kernel thread, so a single blocking system call blocks the entire process with zero multi-core parallelism.
inlineSabotage.why: That is the flaw of the Many-to-One model! One-to-One maps each user thread to its own kernel thread, giving true multi-core parallelism and non-blocking syscalls (§4.3).

bugHunts.prompt: Click the subtly false statement about Processes, fork(), and IPC:
items: 1. Only one process per CPU core can be in the Running state at any given instant.
2. A waiting process transitions directly from the Waiting state back to the Running state as soon as I/O finishes.
3. Shared Memory requires kernel assistance primarily to establish the shared mapping; reads and writes run at RAM speed.
4. An Orphan process whose parent exits early is adopted and reaped by PID 1 (init/systemd).
bugHunts.fix: A process NEVER jumps from Waiting -> Running directly! Upon I/O completion it enters the Ready state and waits for the CPU scheduler (§3.1.2).

bugHunts.type: Code Trace Bug (C fork() & Zombie Check)
bugHunts.prompt: Spot the buggy expectation in this C fork()/wait() snippet:
items: Line 1: pid_t pid = fork();
Line 2: if (pid == 0) { /* Child spawns here; fork() returned positive PID to parent */ }
Line 3: if (pid > 0) { /* Parent spawns here; if parent skips wait() forever after child calls exit(), child becomes an Orphan! */ }
Line 4: else if (pid < 0) { fprintf(stderr, "Fork failed"); }
bugHunts.fix: If the parent is ALIVE and fails to call wait(), the terminated child is a ZOMBIE (not an Orphan!). An Orphan occurs when the parent dies first while the child keeps running (§3.3.2).

socratic.q: Pause & Predict: Executing 3 unconditional `fork(); fork(); fork();` calls produces 8 total processes. What if we run `for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) if (fork() == 0) break;`?
socratic.a: Only the ORIGINAL parent continues looping! Each of the 3 iterations spawns 1 leaf child that immediately hits `break;` -> total = 1 parent + 3 children = 4 processes (not 8!).

socratic.q: Why does Amdahl's Law punish adding 64 cores when 20% of a workload is strictly sequential?
socratic.a: At S = 0.20, Speedup <= 1 / (0.20 + 0.80/64) = 4.7x (and never > 5x even with infinity cores!). Optimizing serial bottlenecks beats throwing cores at code.

inlineSabotage.find: Turnaround Time (TAT — MINIMIZE): Total interval from submission (Arrival) to completion, summing ready-queue wait, CPU bursts, and I/O waits.
inlineSabotage.corrupt: Turnaround Time (TAT — MINIMIZE): Only the cumulative time spent actively executing instructions on the CPU core minus waiting intervals (TAT = CT − WT).
inlineSabotage.why: Turnaround Time measures EVERYTHING from arrival to completion (TAT = CT - AT), INCLUDING ready-queue wait time and I/O wait time! (§5.2).

bugHunts.prompt: Identify the subtly wrong claim about CPU scheduling criteria and circumstances:
items: 1. Scheduling transitions (1) Running -> Waiting and (4) Running -> Terminated must be handled non-preemptively.
2. Dispatch Latency is the time taken by the dispatcher to stop one process and start another running.
3. Waiting Time and Response Time are guaranteed to remain strictly equal for every preemptive Round-Robin schedule.
4. In FCFS, putting a 24ms CPU-bound job before short 3ms jobs causes the Convoy Effect.
bugHunts.fix: WT == RT ONLY when a job gets one uninterrupted CPU burst (non-preemptive). Under preemption (RR, SRTF, Preemptive Priority), a job resumes waiting later, making WT >= RT!

bugHunts.prompt: Given P1(AT=0, BT=8), P2(AT=1, BT=4), P3(AT=2, BT=2) under non-preemptive FCFS, spot the miscalculated line:
items: Line 1: Gantt executes sequentially P1 (0-8), P2 (8-12), P3 (12-14).
Line 2: P1 TAT = 8 - 0 = 8 ms, WT = 8 - 8 = 0 ms.
Line 3: P2 CT = 12 ms, TAT = 12 - 1 = 11 ms, WT = 11 - 4 = 7 ms.
Line 4: P3 CT = 14 ms, TAT = 14 - 0 = 14 ms, WT = 14 - 2 = 12 ms.
bugHunts.fix: P3 arrived at AT = 2 (NOT 0)! Always subtract Arrival Time: TAT(P3) = 14 - 2 = 12 ms, WT(P3) = 12 - 2 = 10 ms!

socratic.q: Pause & Predict: Why does the Convoy Effect hurt DISK / I/O device utilization even though the CPU stays 100% busy?
socratic.a: While the 1 big CPU hog dominates the core, all I/O-bound jobs queue behind it leaving the disk idle; then when it finally blocks on I/O, short jobs rush through CPU in microseconds and all wait together on disk, leaving CPU idle! (§5.3.1)

socratic.q: Under Little's Formula (n = lambda * W), what happens to Ready Queue length if you double arrival rate lambda without speeding up service?
socratic.a: Wait time W explodes non-linearly once utilization reaches saturation, causing queue length n = lambda * W to grow dramatically!

inlineSabotage.find: If α = 0: τn+1 = τn. Recent actual history is completely ignored; initial estimate τ0 rules forever (assumes unchanging process behavior).
inlineSabotage.corrupt: If α = 0: τn+1 = tn. Past history is completely ignored; only the latest actual measured burst tn predicts the next turn.
inlineSabotage.why: You swapped alpha=0 and alpha=1! Setting alpha=0 zeros out t_n so prediction stays frozen at initial tau_0; alpha=1 gives tau_{n+1} = t_n (§5.3.2).

bugHunts.prompt: Click the single false claim about SJF scheduling:
items: 1. SJF is provably optimal in minimizing Average Waiting Time among non-preemptive scheduling algorithms.
2. When two ready processes tie on exact next CPU burst length, SJF breaks the tie using Priority Aging.
3. In exponential averaging with alpha = 0.5, weight falls geometrically as (1 - alpha)^k on older bursts.
4. Long CPU-bound processes can suffer Starvation if short jobs arrive continuously.
bugHunts.fix: Standard SJF tie-breaking ALWAYS uses FCFS (earlier Arrival Time goes first), not Aging! (§5.3.2)

bugHunts.prompt: Find the arithmetic mistake in this Exponential Averaging trace (alpha=0.5, tau_0=10 ms, actual bursts t_0=6, t_1=4):
items: Step 1: Formula is tau_{n+1} = alpha * t_n + (1 - alpha) * tau_n.
Step 3: Next step with t_1 = 4 -> tau_2 = 0.5(4) + 0.5(10) = 2 + 5 = 7 ms.
Step 4: Weight sum alpha + (1 - alpha) always equals 1.0.
bugHunts.fix: Step 3 reused tau_0 (10 ms) instead of tau_1 (8 ms)! Correct math: tau_2 = 0.5(4) + 0.5(8) = 2 + 4 = 6 ms!

socratic.q: Pause & Predict: If a batch job alternates strictly between 10ms and 10ms CPU bursts forever, what happens to tau_n over time when alpha = 0.5 and tau_0 = 100ms?
socratic.a: Difference shrinks by half each burst (100 -> 55 -> 32.5 -> 21.25 -> ...), converging exponentially toward the true mean 10ms!

socratic.q: Why doesn't the Exchange Argument prove FCFS optimal?
socratic.a: Because FCFS forbids moving a shorter job ahead of a longer earlier arrival—only SJF minimizes sum of waits across any permutation of ready jobs.

bugHunts.prompt: Spot the sneaky flaw in these SRTF scheduling statements:
items: 1. SRTF checks for preemption whenever a new process enters the ready queue.
2. If a newly arrived job has Burst == Remaining Burst of the running job, SRTF immediately preempts the running job to improve Response Time.

bugHunts.prompt: Find the misleading textbook claim about Paging and Page Tables:
items: 1. Inverted Page Tables maintain one global table sized proportionally to physical frames rather than virtual pages.
2. Without a TLB, accessing an address through an in-memory single-level page table requires 2 RAM accesses.
3. A 32-bit logical address with 4 KB pages splits into a 12-bit Page Number `p` and a 20-bit Page Offset `d`.
4. Hashed Page Tables are effective for sparse 64-bit virtual address spaces.
bugHunts.fix: BITS REVERSED! Page Size = 4 KB = 2^12 bytes -> lower 12 bits = Offset `d`! Remaining upper 32 - 12 = 20 bits = Page Number `p`! (§9.3.1)

bugHunts.prompt: Spot the math mistake in calculating Effective Access Time (TLB=20ns, RAM=100ns, alpha=80%):
items: Step 1: On TLB HIT (prob = 0.80), time = TLB (20 ns) + RAM Data (100 ns) = 120 ns.
Step 2: On TLB MISS (prob = 0.20), time = TLB (20 ns) + PageTable RAM (100 ns) + Data RAM (100 ns) = 220 ns.
Step 3: Weighted sum: EAT = 0.80 * (120) + 0.20 * (120) = 120 ns.
Step 4: Raising hit rate alpha to 99% drops EAT cleanly to 121 ns.
bugHunts.fix: Step 3 used `120 ns` instead of `220 ns` on the MISS branch! Correct math: `0.80(120) + 0.20(220) = 96 + 44 = 140 ns`! (§9.3.2)

socratic.q: Pause & Predict: Why can't two processes easily share memory pages inside a classic Inverted Page Table without extra kernel machinery?
socratic.a: Because an Inverted Page Table has only ONE slot per physical frame, each containing a single `<pid, page_num>` pair—it cannot map two different processes' virtual pages directly to one slot! (§9.4.3)

socratic.q: Why does 2-level paging (say 10-bit outer p1, 10-bit inner p2, 12-bit offset) save megabytes of RAM for small programs?
socratic.a: You only allocate inner page tables for virtual regions actually used (code + stack + small heap), leaving gigabytes of empty address holes completely unallocated!

bugHunts.prompt: Spot the single false claim about Demand Paging, Replacement, and Thrashing:
items: 1. Copy-on-Write avoids duplicating unmodified parent RAM pages during `fork()` until either process writes.
2. Optimal (OPT) and LRU are Stack Algorithms and can NEVER suffer Belady's Anomaly.
3. Thrashing occurs when total working-set frame demand D exceeds total physical frames m, crashing CPU utilization.
4. Increasing physical frames from 3 to 4 guarantees fewer or equal page faults under ALL page replacement algorithms including FIFO.
bugHunts.fix: BELADY'S ANOMALY! On reference string `1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5`, FIFO actually suffers MORE faults with 4 frames (10) than with 3 frames (9)! Only Stack Algorithms (OPT, LRU) avoid this (§10.4.2).

bugHunts.prompt: Spot the corrupted order/step inside the OS Page Fault Handler:
items: Step A: CPU traps on PTE valid-invalid bit = `i` -> saves registers & checks PCB internal table.
Step B: OS allocates a free physical frame (evicting a victim if RAM full; skipping disk write-back if dirty == 0!).
Step C: Schedules disk read into frame while process moves to Waiting state.
Step D: On disk interrupt, update PTE bit `i -> v`, and resume execution at the NEXT instruction SKIPPING the trapped opcode!
bugHunts.fix: NEVER skip the instruction! The trapped memory load/store never succeeded before the fault! Step 6 MUST RESTART THE EXACT TRAPPED INSTRUCTION cleanly so the read/write executes now that the page is in RAM (§10.2.1)!

socratic.q: Pause & Predict: Why does Enhanced Second-Chance Clock search `(ref, modify)` pairs in exact order `(0,0) -> (0,1) -> (1,0) -> (1,1)`?
socratic.a: `(0,0)` was neither recently used NOR modified (zero disk write-back needed = free victim!). `(0,1)` wasn't recently used, needs write-back. `(1,0)` was used recently but clean. `(1,1)` is worst (recently used AND dirty)!

socratic.q: When Thrashing hits, why does a naive scheduler that adds MORE jobs whenever CPU utilization drops make Thrashing catastrophically worse?
socratic.a: Low CPU utilization happens because processes are blocked WAITING ON SWAP DISK, NOT idle waiting for CPU! Swapping in more processes shrinks everyone's frame count further, multiplying page faults!

bugHunts.prompt: Find the broken engineering statement among these Mass Storage facts:
items: 1. NAND Flash SSDs must erase an entire multi-page Erase Block before overwriting updated pages, requiring Wear Leveling.
2. SSTF minimizes local seek distance greedily, creating a risk of Starvation for extreme outer/inner cylinder requests.
3. C-SCAN services requests both on its upward sweep AND on its rapid downward return sweep back toward cylinder 0.
4. For 6 x 4TB disks, RAID 5 gives 20TB (1 fail tolerance) while RAID 6 gives 16TB (2 simultaneous fail tolerance).
bugHunts.fix: C-SCAN treats the disk circularly: it services ONLY in ONE direction (e.g., UP 53 -> 199), then returns immediately `199 -> 0` WITHOUT servicing any requests during the return sweep! (Doing both directions is bidirectional SCAN!) (§11.2.3).

socratic.q: Pause & Predict: Why does RAID 1+0 (Stripe of Mirrors) outperform RAID 0+1 (Mirror of Stripes) in reliability when 2 random drives fail across a 4-disk array?
socratic.a: In RAID 0+1, if 1 disk fails in Left Stripe, the whole Left Stripe fails; losing ANY drive in Right Stripe destroys the array (4/6 two-drive pairs kill it!). In RAID 1+0, losing 1 drive from Pair A leaves Pair A mirrored; ONLY losing Pair A's exact partner destroys it (only 2/6 pairs kill it!) (§11.8.3).

socratic.q: For a 7,200 RPM HDD transferring a 4 KB block across tracks vs. an NVMe SSD, why are OS Disk Scheduling algorithms like SCAN/SSTF mostly disabled (`none`/`noop`) for NVMe SSDs?
socratic.a: SSDs have zero mechanical seek arm or spinning platter! All NAND channels answer uniformly in microseconds regardless of LBA cylinder address (§11.1.2).

bugHunts.prompt: Click the single false claim about Disk Allocation & File Systems:

bugHunts.fix: That describes a SYMBOLIC (SOFT) LINK! A UNIX Hard Link points directly to the shared Inode number with an incremented reference count (`link_count`), never creating dangling text paths (§13.3.4).

bugHunts.type: Inode Max File Size Math Bug (4KB Block, 4B Pointer = 1024 Ptrs/Blk)
bugHunts.prompt: Find the order-of-magnitude bug in calculating max file size for a UNIX Inode (12 Direct + 1 Single + 1 Double + 1 Triple Indirect, 4KB blocks, 4B ptrs):
items: Line 1: Pointers per Index Block P = 4,096 B / 4 B = 1,024 = 2^10 pointers.
Line 2: 12 Direct Blocks = 12 * 4 KB = 48 KB.
Line 3: 1 Single Indirect = 1,024 * 4 KB = 4 MB; 1 Double Indirect = (1,024)^2 * 4 KB = 4 GB.
Line 4: 1 Triple Indirect = (1,024)^3 * 4 B = 4 GB -> Total Max File Size ~ 8 GB!
bugHunts.fix: Multiply data block count `(1024)^3` by **4 KB** (4,096 B per data block), NOT by 4 Bytes (pointer size)! Correct: `2^30 * 4 KB = 4 TB` (~4.004 TB total) (§14.4.3)!

socratic.q: Pause & Predict: Suppose OS Buffer Cache and Virtual Memory Page Cache sit separately in kernel RAM. What bug/waste occurs when calling `read()` on a file simultaneously `mmap()`-ed into virtual memory?
socratic.a: DOUBLE CACHING! Two identical copies of the same disk file sit in RAM simultaneously (one in Buffer Cache, one in Page Cache), risking inconsistency and halving effective cache RAM—cured by Unified Buffer Cache (§14.6.2)!

bugHunts.prompt: Find the erroneous statement in these I/O Systems claims:
items: 1. Memory-Mapped I/O maps controller registers directly into physical RAM address space for fast graphics/NVMe writes.
2. Polling (Programmed I/O) beats Interrupt-Driven I/O when ultra-fast device latency is shorter than interrupt dispatch overhead.
3. Spooling queues exclusive jobs onto disk spool files so multiple users don't interleave lines on a shared printer.
4. A Kernel Cache may hold the sole existing copy of an item in transit, whereas a Kernel Buffer strictly copies data stored permanently elsewhere.
bugHunts.fix: REVERSED DEFINITIONS (§12.4.3)! A **Buffer** holds data in transit and may hold the ONLY copy of an item; a **Cache** strictly holds a faster temporary copy of data stored safely elsewhere!

bugHunts.type: I/O API Mode Check (Blocking vs Nonblocking vs Async)
bugHunts.prompt: Match each syscall trace to its exact Silberschatz §12.3.4 semantics—click the mismatched line:
items: Blocking read(): Calling thread suspends inside Waiting Queue until controller completes transfer and copies data into user buffer.
Nonblocking read(): Returns immediately with whatever bytes currently reside in kernel buffer (even 0 / EAGAIN).
Asynchronous read(): Returns immediately so app computes concurrently, and kernel signals app ONLY AFTER the full transfer finishes.
Copy Semantics bug: Asynchronous write() needs Double Buffering because nonblocking reads never use kernel buffers.
bugHunts.fix: Kernel uses **Copy Semantics** (copying user write-buffer into a private kernel buffer at call time) so if the app modifies its own array immediately after calling async `write()`, the disk still gets the clean snapshot as of the call instant! (§12.4.2)

socratic.q: Pause & Predict: During DMA Cycle Stealing, does the CPU halt completely until the 4 KB disk transfer ends?
socratic.a: NO! The DMA controller borrows only the memory bus cycles between CPU cache/register instructions; the CPU continues executing compute instructions inside registers/L1/L2 cache seamlessly! (§12.2.4)

socratic.q: Why must ALL direct I/O port instructions (`IN`/`OUT` or memory-mapped control writes) remain strictly privileged Kernel-Mode instructions?
socratic.a: If User Mode could issue raw controller commands, a malicious app could overwrite disk sector 0 (partition table / OS kernel) or sniff other processes' keystrokes bypassing file permissions!

bugHunts.prompt: Spot the subtly corrupted statement about OS Security & Protection:
items: 1. Access Control Lists (ACLs) store permissions column-wise with each object, making per-file user revocation immediate.
2. Capability Lists store unforgeable tokens row-wise with each protection domain, making immediate selective revocation harder.
3. A Digital Signature encrypts a document hash using the sender's PUBLIC key so anyone claiming to be the sender can decrypt it.

bugHunts.fix: Digital Signatures MUST encrypt the digest `Hash(M)` with the sender's **PRIVATE Key**! Anyone can verify using the sender's Public Key—proving ONLY the private-key holder could have signed it (§16.4.1.3)!

socratic.q: Pause & Predict: Why can a Network Worm replicate across thousands of machines automatically without human clicking, unlike a classic File Virus?
socratic.a: A Virus is parasitic code attached to a host executable requiring users to share/run files; a Worm is a standalone network process exploiting remote vulnerabilities (like buffer overflows) over TCP/IP autonomously! (§16.2.3)

socratic.q: How do NX/DEP and ASLR work together like a two-layer lock against Stack Buffer Overflows?
socratic.a: Even if an overflow overwrites the Saved Return Address, NX blocks executing injected shellcode on the stack, AND ASLR randomizes libc/gadget memory addresses so Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) jumps miss blindly! (§16.6.7)
